PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
As hon. members will have noticed, there are on today's order paper almost 100 public bills listed lor introduction by private members. It would be difficult il not impossible for the Chair to review the provisions of these bills at this time. In view of that fact, may I suggest to the House that we adopt the procedure which was agreed upon by the House in the past two sessions, namely that we proceed to the introduction and first reading of these bills so that each may be scrutinized between now and the time appointed for second reading in order to determine whether there be any defect therein with respect to the practices and usages of the House.
Therefore, in order to save the time of the House, taking into consideration that perhaps more than two hours would be required to introduce each of these measures separately, it is suggested that, by unanimous consent, all the bills listed for introduction on today's order paper be deemed to have been introduced, given first reading and ordered for second reading at the next sitting of the house, subject of course to a subsequent examination as to the regularity of each bill.
Is it agreed?

subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, in respect of a matter of this importance I am not going to indulge in idle comment. I think my right hon. friend and the House generally will agree that the discussion which the Prime Minister had with the President last Saturday was a useful one. I believe that the President's speech last night took into account important suggestions that had been made to him from many quarters, and it is clear from some of the proposals that the conversation of the Prime Minister of Canada with the President was indeed a very useful and fortunate one at that particular moment.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
While I am on my feet I should like to say that the Canadian government welcomes
22620-7 j
Inquiries of the Ministry President Johnson's proposal for a greatly expanded co-operative effort for economic development in Southeast Asia to be initiated under the United Nations. Some weeks ago there was mention made of a development scheme for the Mekong. Because of Canada's initial interest in this program we have been thinking along much the same lines as the President and are prepared to play our full part in contributing to the success of this plan.
It will be recalled that on Friday night the Prime Minister, speaking at Temple University, made specific suggestions for such an expanded co-operative effort. The Canadian government stands ready to designate a special representative to join with the Secretary General of the United Nations and representatives of other industrialized countries to help in the preparation of the plan and in mobilizing the necessary additional resources. I am happy to note that the President is establishing a special United States team to be headed by Mr. Eugene Black, the distinguished former President of the World Bank. The government shares the hope that all other industrialized countries, including the Soviet Union and, I might add, eventually China, will contribute to this common endeavour and that, as soon as peaceful co-operation is possible, North Viet Nam could take its place in the co-operative effort.
Canada is particularly fitted to play a role because of our long association with many of the countries of Southeast Asia, our participation in co-operative peace and development efforts in the area. Because of the character of the Indochina countries our bicultural heritage will be of considerable advantage. I should like to say that we have asked our Ambassador at the United Nations to come to Ottawa-he came last night-to discuss with us certain proposals that we will make to the Secretary General in connection with the proposal made by the President with regard to this scheme for co-operative development in Southeast Asia.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in putting a supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs perhaps I might be pardoned for saying that we welcome the statement of Canada's willingness to take part in this commitment in Southeast Asia. I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if the Canadian government is planning to follow up another aspect of the President's speech in which he said that the United States was ready for unconditional discussions leading to a final settlement. I was wondering if Canada proposed to take any specific steps with regard to this aspect of the President's speech.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVINCIAL OWNERSHIP OF SHARES IN CHARTERED BANKS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: SPEECH BY U.S. PRESIDENT RESPECTING SOUTHEAST ASIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government is available for discussions at any time. Indeed, we have discussions with the United States in one form or another almost daily. What is now required is that the other side should be prepared to enter into discussions. There was a notable statement in the President's speech when he said that the United States was prepared to enter into discussions without any preconditions.
I am now in a position to say, having sought clarification of that speech, that a cease fire would not be a condition precedent to the initiation of discussions which, as the President said, were being offered unconditionally. On the other hand, the President said any settlement would have to meet certain requirements involving the independence of South Viet Nam. In other words there do seem to be conditions for a settlement, but not for the beginning of discussions.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL OWNERSHIP OF SHARES IN CHARTERED BANKS

maintopic: PROVINCIAL OWNERSHIP OF SHARES IN CHARTERED BANKS

speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot comment on policy in the United States. My hon. friend asks if this represents a change of policy, but I cannot be expected to comment on that. Likewise I cannot say what the policy of Hanoi is unless it is given clearly, and it has not been given. With regard to pre-conditions, when we were presented with the Belgrade appeal of the 17 nations, I said, on behalf of the Government, there was much in that appeal we could support. One element was the absence of pre-conditions with regard to the holding of peace talks.

I shared also their desire, as I am sure all hon. members do, that negotiations for a peaceful and honourable settlement should begin immediately if possible. I did not, I must add, see eye to eye with them in their entire assessment of the responsibilities and reasons for the present situation.

In view of all these very promising plans we heard from the President of the United States, and which receive general support in this House, can the Minister now tell us, since all these plans are predicated on the existence of the United Nations, if we can take it
April 8, 1965

from the announcement of the President of the United States that the impasse in the United Nations is likely to be broken in the near future; and can the Minister tell us how negotiations are getting along in connection with the opening of the new Assembly in respect of a vote taking place?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROVINCIAL OWNERSHIP OF SHARES IN CHARTERED BANKS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
I fail to see any
relationship between the facts stated and the suggestion of the President, supported by the Canadian Prime Minister, that the Secretary General of the United Nations should use his good offices to further the development of this co-operative economic aid program under the auspices of the United Nations. speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cashin for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we were reminded by the reading of the speech from the throne, we are now beginning a new session. May I offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for having highlighted, according to the views of their party, the main points
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Marcoux that will come up for discussion during this new period in the life of the twenty sixth parliament.
The proposals brought before us by the government are far-reaching and we may well wonder whether it is realistic to imagine that we could go through such of heavy program during the next few months, especially when the government is in a minority position.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on this twenty sixth parliament which, while it did not give us a majority government, has just the same provided a stable administration. In the first place, let us not forget that the present representation in the House of Commons obviously reflects the state of mind of Canadians from coast to coast. The democratic system allowing for a free vote, it seems that the Canadian electors did not see enough outstanding qualities in any party to give them an absolute majority. And I think that such a situation will continue for several years to come.
Governments will have to get used to such a way of life. Like a person suffering from diabetes or from a heart condition who has to make the best of his illness, our government will have to recognize that the days of all-powerful administrations are definitely past. However, we must admit that in spite of defects and infirmities, the life expectancy is not necessarily shorter, quite the contrary. But that is a far cry from saying that no cooperation is necessary.
Many take pleasure in saying that others- not them indeed-have tarnished the image of the House of Commons. Newspapermen from coast to coast have been saying that parliament is on the downgrade. Despite all the reservations I often make in regard to newspapermen, 1 must nevertheless admit that it is here indeed that they form an opinion about parliament, and not outside the house. When they charge the opposition with filibustering, it is certainly because idle discussions go on and on, that we mark time and that no new ideas are brought forward. Even if a party blames another for doing everything to achieve its purpose, it will become as guilty when it also resorts to such tactics.
And, Mr. Speaker, this brings me to discuss the conception that certain politicians have of public as well as personal morality. It seems that the basic principles of natural law are more and more ignored. Instead of being guided by those principles, those politicians readily come to take an everybody-is-

doing-it attitude. While yesterday fraud and theft were considered as sins against natural law, the trend today is to greater tolerance because many people commit such wrongdoings. In the past, people used to say adulterers, but today they say "common law spouse"; formerly, respect for justice was the order of the day, but today freedom not to abide by it is claimed. And I could go on.
How is it that individuals attempt to exert pressures on public men for the sole purpose of lining their own pockets? Is it conceivable that alleged guilty persons would try to buy their innocence? Why is it that many persons are under the impression that politicians can tamper with the administration of justice? Are there any reasons why one should think that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor? Is it because some individuals have uncovered some secret dealings and want to be treated like certain privileged persons?
Why is the member of parliament consulted as if he were a lawyer and why is he expected to espouse the cause of his so-called client? Apparently some people thought the climate was favourable to such dealings and resolved to try to benefit therefrom, no wonder that there are so many partisans and parasites around. Is it any wonder then that the underworld, seeking protection against the administration of justice, the law and the authorities, joins hands with political hangers-on-particularly those who gravitate around the party in office-hoping to influence them.
Public administration is usually considered as the art of governing and the latter as the art of making things come true. His Worship Mayor Jean Drapeau, of Montreal, even said that it was the art of bringing into being the things that are necessary. That is all very well. But from a partisan point of view, politics can be quite a different proposition. And I fully agree with this statement I have heard: Politics is the art of getting into office and remaining there. The large number of parties we now have and the powerful opposition will have at least served to bring the government to pay more attention to its role as administrator and forget about partisanship.
However, the speech from the throne shows the eagerness of the Liberal party to cater to the electorate. They bow to the pressures exerted, they yield to the demands of intermediate groups. They no longer care whether the principles of Christian democracy are safeguarded; they no longer seek the objective criteria which should continue to guide
April 8. 1965

our actions. No, they try to compromise on a middle-of-the-road policy-which is not always the right one-between the age-long interests of financiers and swindlers, while endeavouring to soothe the people with phoney presents.
As a former Liberal prime minister said, "Not necessarily conscription but conscription if necessary", today they say "Not necessarily socialism but socialism if necessary".
I do not imply by this that social measures are not useful. On the contrary, our party has been advocating this imperative necessity for more than 30 years. What we fear is the increasingly larger place our governments are taking in the life of the individuals. We believe in maintaining the freedom of individuals and businesses, not the freedom of gangsters, outlaws, monopolizers, trusts, tyrants or dishonest people. Unfortunately, when persons speak along these lines, they are readily called reactionaries. Attempts are made to picture them as people who oppose progress and experiments.
Nothing is farther from the truth or more malicious. But I believe that it is the part of wisdom to warn against making any change in our system without scrutinizing it beforehand. Otherwise, we might become unable to back out of such changes without difficulty. When we see how painfully the government makes a show of letting the provinces opt out of joint programs, especially on account of the huge organization of civil servants necessitated by centralization, we immediately realize how it is almost impossible to reverse the trend in the social field, even if we are conscious of being in a false position. Let us remember that the former labour prime minister of Great Britain, Lord Attlee, said in February 1947 that there was a basic difference between totalitarian planning and suggestive economic planning. Like everyone else, he did not dare go forward blindly into dictatorial state control. Well, less than six months after that statement, the Labour government had to recommend labour conscription.
In saying that, I do not accuse all socialists of deliberately trying to set up a totalitarian regime; however, I should like to point out that socialist planning bears within itself a germ which will lead to serious but inevitable consequences.
The government has stated that it will consider the establishment of health services for Canadian citizens. Does it mean that our compatriots are unable to look after their 22620-8J

The proponents of socialism claim that private enterprise has been subjected to the whims and fantasies of a few irresponsible people. According to them, planning is essential to general welfare. To achieve such a high standard of perfection in the establishment of various health services, private enterprise must have undertaken intensive planning and multiply consultations with the various bodies concerned.
It must not be forgotten that the general interest of a people, the common good, cannot be measured on a scale. It is imperative that the common needs and interest be examined at various levels by the proper agencies of intermediate organizations where each need of each human person must be placed in its own context. Totalitarian and executory state planning seems therefore inconsistent with the adequate working of true democracy.
It should also be noted that an undue state control really affects the people in the end. It is most important to bring about a psychological change, to alter the character of the population. This is done gradually and brings forth new attitudes toward authority. When complete planning has firmly taken hold of each member of the community it moulds them at will, albeit with the best intention in the world. It catches society as a whole in a huge net of minute complicated and standard rules which practically prevent the people from acting intelligently.
After sincerely claiming to be the people's protector, one eventually becomes a tyrant. Will-power is not destroyed or crushed, but it is softened, moulded and controlled. It cannot be said that man is forced to act, but he is constantly prevented from acting and reacting. Such a power of the state does not suppress life, but it prevents it. It does not really tyrannize, but it compresses, emasculates, stifles, stupefies a people, until the nation becomes a herd of scared pack-animals. We can stop wondering why so few voices are

Perhaps some will say that I should not take things so tragically, but I suggest it is normal, fitting and wise to stop and think, review the situation and contemplate what any change in our way of life could bring us in the long run. Since the Soviet Union has reached the summit of communism, that is the socialist state, it is perfectly natural to study the conditions that exist in countries behind the iron curtain. I feel it is foolish not to consider all avenues while pretending to wish to take people out of their misery and poverty.
And let us not forget that totalitarianism can come by different ways, even if it all amounts to the same results. It is of no importance to me whether we have a nazi, fascist or communist dictatorship. I do not want any of them. Regimes such as Japan, Italy and Germany used to have are of no more appeal to me than those found today in Russia, East Germany, Cuba and elsewhere. In my opinion, they all end up by creating a great big herd of slaves. And it can only be a good thing to try and find the reasons why state interventions will produce results that perhaps one did not seek.
What is wrong, is the well organized, arranged, and indeed, extremely well planned movement to allow our economic life to be controlled by the state which would eventually and inevitably become the main owner of production means. This is true socialism.
I do not mean to imply that our present system is perfect. On the contrary, and for over 30 years, our party has been thundering against the abuses of capitalism, objecting against its materialism. As a matter of fact, I consider our present system as an economic dictatorship, as hateful as any other. It surely does not reflect much credit on our system that segregation and discrimination could still exist in America and that poverty is still rampant.
But we must at all costs guard against the danger of being so impatient to obtain quick results as to select means, as useful as they might be in the near or distant future, which are inconsistent with the preservation of a truly free society.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a point that has been sys-

tematically overlooked since 1958: family allowances. At that time, before the election, as it happened, during the consideration of the 1957-58 supplementary estimates, a provision was included as a clause in the supply bill, so as to increase by $1 the allowances paid at the time. What an improvement.
When they were established under chapter 40, 1944-45, so-called responsible people jeered at large families and even made so bold as to suggest that such allowances would encourage the bestiality of parents. As if those allowances would be enough to support a child, even a baby. Well, Mr. Speaker, it seems that many people still hold this view, because no one can bring the government to comply with the rightful demands of the fathers and mothers of large or small families.
And here is why we ask that the Bank of Canada be used to increase those allowances. Allow me to repeat some points of law since some hon. members seem unconvinced still. If you refer to the Bank of Canada Act, chapter 43, 1934, you will find that it is not granted any power to issue bank credit. But section 21 gives it the exclusive right to issue bank notes which constitute legal tender. Section 24 stipulated that chartered banks had to maintain a reserve but it was abrogated by section 11 of the act amending the Bank of Canada Act, chapter 33, 1954. Therefore, it is necessary to refer to the Bank Act, chapter 48, 1954, to find out what liquidities the chartered banks have to maintain, that is what amounts in bank notes of the Bank of Canada, in addition to the money deposited with the Bank of Canada, chartered banks must keep on hand to create a $100 credit. Under section 71 of the Bank Act, that cash reserve must not be lower than $8, which means that each $100 loan granted by a chartered bank must be covered by $8 in cash. That provision means, therefore, that under the act chartered banks are authorized to loan 12J times more money than they have on hand.
I ask this question. Why should not the Bank of Canada be authorized also to loan to the Canadian government 12J times the amount of the deposits it has on hand? It is not a matter of preventing chartered banks from helping the small people as well as the big companies; it is only a matter of applying to the Bank of Canada those principles which are good for the chartered banks. It would encourage the general development of our country instead of benefiting only a small group of privileged
April 8, 1965

people. To solve in this way social problems, Mr. Speaker, that is not socialism but simply the application to the common good of a system that has always well served particular interests.
So as to show you that this is really a fault of capitalism in general, may I quote from a pamphlet entitled "Money Facts" and published on September 21, 1964 by the United States government for the committee on banking and money of the House of Representatives.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)

On page 1 we find question No. 3:
Why is the money-creating power important?
This is the answer:
Because, by creating money, banks provide the exchange media which the economy needs to prosper and grow. Since the growth and proper functioning of the U.S. economy require increasing amounts of money over the years, those who control the amount of money exercise great power over business activity, the incomes people earn, and our economic strength.
Page 2, question No. 7:
What problems are raised by an "independent" Federal Reserve?
The answer is:
There are two major problems. One is the problem of political responsibility for the country's economic policies. The other is the problem of final control over the government's actions in the economic sphere.
Page 5, question No. 22:
What is money?
The answer is:
Money is anything that people will accept in exchange for goods or services, in the belief that they may, in turn, exchange it, now or later, for other goods or services. Any number of different materials-including paper i.o.u.'s-may serve as money. How money functions, and what money represents are its important aspects and not simply what it is made of.
Page 12, question No. 69:
If the government can issue bonds, why can't it issue money and save the interest?
This is the answer:
A few clear headed and firm individuals, such as Abraham Lincoln, have insisted that the government should. The late Thomas A. Edison stated the matter this way:
"If our nation can issue a dollar bond it can issue a dollar bill. The element that makes the bond good makes the bill good also. It is absurd to say that our country can issue $30 million in bonds and not $30 million in currency. Both are promises to pay: but one promise fattens the usurer and the other helps the people."

The Address-Mr. Marcoux
However, it has long been one of the political facts of life that private banks must be allowed to create the lion's share of the money, even if not all of the money. Thus there is little opposition to the government's printing bonds and then permitting the banks to create the money with which to buy those bonds; but proposals that the government itself create the money instead of the bonds have always set off tremendous political upheavals. For example, Abraham Lincoln set off a political furor when he insisted upon having the government issue $346 million in money, the so-called "greenbacks", instead of issuing interest bearing bonds and paying interest on the money.
Page 29, question 155:
Isn't the suggestion of improving the money system both impudent and a call for needless tinkering with the economy?
This is the answer:
Not at all. The monetary system of today, improved as it has been over the past 200 or so years, is still man made. There is no reason to conclude that the system is perfect. The process of improving the money system is not complete any more than is the process of improving our national life generally.
Further, in every period of our history, people, especially bankers, have resisted any change in our money system with the cry, "leave well enough alone." Then some disaster would strike and the monetary system would be changed in panic and haste. The system always looks solid or at least adequate until the moment it becomes inadequate. The fact that the system is now functioning more or less satisfactorily is no reason to shun inspection. Economic health and progress is the result of continual care and attention.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read question No. 157:
In practical terms, what is meant by Federal Reserve "independence"?
This is the answer:
There are two sides to independence-one is economic, the other political. On the economic side, independence means that the Federal Reserve formulates and executes economic policy, using its monetary controls, without any necessary reference or co-ordination with the policies being followed by the other branches of the government. This, of course, invites clashes between the Federal Reserve and other parts of the government.

wish to take up too much time in commenting directly on the Speech from the Throne, since I have a few other matters to bring to the attention of the House. Members of the House and all members of the Press Gallery will welcome the change. Surely the change will put new life into Parliamentary debate. I look for not just shorter but sharper comment and wit in this House as a result, and I hope this proposal will be introduced by the Government and agreed to at the earliest possible date.
We hear a lot in this House and elsewhere these days, Mr. Speaker, about what is going on in Quebec. We hear about biculturalism and bilingualism; we hear of French Canadian rights under the British North America Act; we hear of the quiet revolution, and so on. Representatives such as myself from the western part of Canada are fortunate in being close to the action, since we can see probably more clearly than those who are not so close just what is going on. However, our position carries with it the responsibility for interpreting to our constituents what it is we do see. It is our clear and, I think, pleasant duty to report back to them, and on this subject we can in truth say that an old era is passing and with it is going a great deal that should have long since departed.
When the hasty words and wild actions of the fanatics and men of ill will have been rewarded with the public contempt they so fully deserve, and when in the calm atmosphere of tolerance we take a good look at the activities of the genuine Quebecker, we can see very clearly what he is working for. What he is building is surely his share, his rightful share, of something we have all been giving lip service to in word and song for many a long year, a land strong and freed, a land with a future that will be proud and respected.
Few of us can have any argument with this objective, and I know that most Westerners will wish Quebeckers the best of good luck. All Canada will be the stronger when this quiet revolution gets up a really good head of steam. It is a very poor imitation Canadian whose heart does not beat just a little bit faster when he visits la belle Province and its great city of Montreal. He sees for himself what his fellow countrymen are achieving down there these days. What the French Canadians are doing for themselves in the Province of Quebec will unquestionably stimulate lively discussion in the rest of Canada. It already has, and what is wrong with that? I am sure that with imagination and good sense, fortunately present in such abundance on both sides, we will all survive and be the better for it.
I wish now to speak on two other matters to which I regretfully found no reference in

the Throne Speech. The first concerns inflation and the second the up-dating of pensions for retired Federal Government civil employees and military personnel.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that no one group in our society is more aware of the dangers and effects of inflation than pensioners. No group is more ill equipped to fight the continuous day to day battles of inflation than retired public servants and their widows. I think it is because of our mild climate in Victoria and our generally civilized outlook on life-if you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, for referring to it in those terms- that we have living in Victoria a large percentage of retired persons, including large numbers of retired military personnel and civil servants, o (12:40 p.m.)
I wish to make a special appeal for consideration of their problems. With so many on the front benches who have been employees of the Federal Government themselves at one time or another before entering this House, I cannot help but feel that my plea will not fall on deaf ears. I doubt that anyone would dare claim that Government employees generally, be they civil or military, have been overpaid in the past for the work they have done. The military and the federal civil service have been and still are among our nation's most loyal and trusted servants. They have an international reputation for their ability which is second to none, and it grieves me to see how they fare at the hands of the nation after their retirement. With pensions wedded or welded-call it what you will-to the rates of pay they were receiving at the time of their retirement, there is no-I repeat, no- provision for the implacable, gnawing away effects of inflation, an inflation which the Government is apparently unable to prevent.
This being the case, Mr. Speaker-and I do not argue this point; I am not one of those who believe that the Government can control inflation without at the same time imposing a host of other wholly unacceptable and undesirable controls-I think the Federal Government has a responsibility toward their faithful and on this point largely helpless, servants to provide decent pensions as a matter of right-having been honestly earned -at a rate, I suggest, that is at least in step with the up to date salaries or wages paid by the Government for the same work today.
Surely this is not too much to ask. It is not even striking into new ground, because the same principle has been followed for
April 8, 1965

years by the government in the land to the south of us, and to a certain extent it is also being followed across the sea today in the United Kingdom. If we cannot strike out on our own with a new, improved formula, can we not at least follow in their footsteps? We might even want to tie federal pensions to the cost of living index; and this is another approach which would be quite all right with me.
I am very encouraged to see in the Canada Pension Plan that the Government for the first time has done something along this line, and has provided automatic increases in pension payments with increases in the cost of living index. I commend the Government wholeheartedly for this. If the Government does not want to take the course of action that I recommended just now to provide fair, up to date pensions, then by all means let us regard the Canada Pension Plan as a precedent and tie our federal pensions in with the cost of living index. I do not mind which course we follow; but we must, in my view, do something. What I wish to impress upon the Government is that the time is far past when we should have made this move. Successive governments have fumbled, waffled and ignored their pensioners long enough, and Provincial Governments and private employers have not been slow, as we all know, to follow suit.
If I may make an observation at this point, Mr. Speaker, I think federal pensioners generally have been much too quiet on the subject of their inflation-caused pension troubles. This is perhaps natural. With years of public service ingrained in their lives, after retirement they have for the most part sat patiently by and watched their hard earned pensions slowly but surely being eaten away by inflation, hoping the Government in its role of Great White Father will do the right thing by them.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that bitter experience has shown them that their confidence has been misplaced. This is a lesson that should not be lost on the federal civil service of today, particularly when they approach the bargaining table for the first time this year, as I am happy to see was promised in the Throne Speech. Nothing can be more frustrating than to see salaries increase year by year across the land, taking care of rising costs for those fortunate enough and young enough to be still employed, while at the same time pensioners experience those same rising costs but are caught in the vise-like grip of a fixed pension.
The Address-Mr. Starr
At present there is no way out for them, Mr. Speaker. Retirement sentences the public servant to a gradual lowering of living standards, and the spectre of an eventual appeal to welfare or charity of one sort or another is a distinct possibility in all too many cases. Members should ask themselves the question, is this fair and is this right? These people do not require alms or handouts; they do need help, and help to them is most justly due. As a Federal Government it is both our moral responsibility and in our own best interests to provide it; for if we are going to attract good people into the service of our country- and, looking ahead, I suggest this is as important today as ever before in our history- we must show that at the end of such service there is a fair retirement.
Surely this fits in with Liberal thinking- spell it as you wish, with a large or a small letter "L"-for the Federal Government to show the way, to provide the lead for provincial and private employers in protecting the purchasing power and the retirement way of life of its faithful servants. I hope, therefore, that the Government will remember its responsibility, will look closely into this problem without delay and will take action very shortly during this Parliament to bring an end to this sorry situation.

One has to examine this speech very carefully to find what new legislation the Government intends to bring forward during this Session of Parliament. This Speech reminds me of the speech made by President Johnson, because it has been dubbed as the speech of war on poverty, and I think this has been done purposely.
This Speech also reminds me of the 60 days of decision used by this Government as its slogan when it first came into office, which slogan was modelled on the late President Kennedy's motto of 90 days of decision. The only variation is the difference of 30 days. This Speech is nothing but a manifesto of words, when we come to look at it very closely. To my mind this Government has copied the actions, the words and the platforms of the Democratic Party of the United States now on two occasions; first, those of the late President Kennedy, and now those of President Johnson. I am wondering when this Government is going to come forward with some of its own ideas, and when it is going to tell the people of Canada that it is prepared to stand on its own two feet rather than mimic the actions of the Government of the United States.
I am also wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether any action is going to result from the listing of some of the things which are embodied in this Speech, because very few

of the matters listed in the last Speech from the Throne which we debated in this House came about. It is true that the Government make a practice of adding words to present legislation. When they talked about certain aspects of legislation which is now on the books of the country in the last Speech they said this was to be "improved", a word which meant nothing at all. They now apply a different adjective to legislation which is presently on the books and already in existence. The 60 days of decision was a complete fraud and a flop during the last session of parliament, and we now expect that the pious platitudes which have been set out in this Throne Speech will experience the same fate.
The war on poverty is a very interesting title for this Speech from the Throne because, as we have noticed in the past session of parliament, cabinet minister after cabinet minister in this Government, particularly outside of the House of Commons on public platforms, has declared that things were very much better, that the Government had solved the economic problems, and that things were on the move. It is strange that now in the Speech from the Throne we find the admission by this Government that there is poverty in Canada, and that they are going to wage a war on that poverty. I will deal with the various items the Government propose in order to eliminate poverty as I go through the Speech. I am wondering whether the war on poverty, as I say, is an admission that nothing has been done since this Government came into office two years ago to rectify the situation.
Let us see, Mr. Speaker, what the Throne Speech contains. First of all there is a reference in one paragraph of the Speech to the automobile agreement which was signed by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada. Let us look at the situation created by this agreement. First of all, it was agreed that Canada would forgo on new parts and new automobiles coming into Canada duties ranging anywhere from 17J per cent to 25 per cent. Under this agreement the United States also agreed to forgo up to 8J per cent duty on all parts and automobiles being shipped into the United States.
As I understand it, 50 per cent of the power to forgo this duty lies in the initiative of the President of the United States; the balance, the other 50 per cent, lies in the Congress of the United States. It was

decided that the President of the United States would not exercise his part of the power to reduce the duty on these automobiles and parts going into the United States, but rather would wait until Congress had approved the agreement so the whole remission could be made at once. On the other hand, Canada immediately implemented her part of that agreement without coming to Parliament for approval of any kind. This was done either by Order in Council or by decision of the Cabinet. The Government were anxious to get into this agreement, but up until now it has been a one way agreement which has been implemented by Canada but not by the United States.

The Speech from the Throne is no better nor worse than those we are accustomed to hear, except that it contains disturbing admissions which point to the weakness of an administration that failed to anticipate or settle the problems of an expanding nation. Government by the old-line parties has been an obstacle to this country's development and the welfare of its population, in that it has left too many people in dire poverty. The government has just realized it as evidenced by the speech from the throne; however, there are two rather contradictory paragraphs which I will quote. First:
Our country is achieving a high rate of economic growth. Trade is expanding. With the growing industrialization, Canadians are enjoying rapidly increasing employment opportunities; incomes and living standards are rising; the number of people out of work has been reduced to lower levels than for many years.
And the next paragraph continues:
All the great potentialities of our economy are not, however, being realized. The talents of some of our people are wasted because of poverty, illness, inadequate education and training, inequality in opportunities for work.
While the economic growth of some favoured classes of society is praised, it is recognized that a great mass of the population are becoming poorer and poorer; fortunately the government has just realized it. But what does it propose in this connection? For some, the situation has improved; for others, it has considerably deteriorated. The number of poor, poverty stricken and needy people has kept on increasing, and what does the government propose? Long term measures: to study the situation of the poor man, find out why he is poor.
In Health and Welfare of January 1965, published under the authority of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh), there is an article entitled:
Fight against indigence.
It is subtitled:
Canada attacks one of the great social evils of today.


I would like to quote the beginning of this article.
In Ottawa, on a day in November of last year, about 50 people met to launch an attack against poverty, which is probably today's greatest social evil. The group was made up of experts from the federal civil service, universities, labour unions and social welfare agencies; they were all deeply worried about continuing poverty in Canada. They all knew that poverty exists. Many of them had seen appalling evidence of it; several were engaged in studies and research to find out the reasons for it; others were working to alleviate it. But they all agreed that a more thorough investigation was needed to gather all information available and discover what information was still needed.
It was felt that not enough information was available to determine what is poverty and want.
Among this group of people who met in November last, nobody was found to be sufficiently informed or intelligent enough, nor could such people be found elsewhere in Canada. That is why it was found necessary to ask another country, England, to come to our rescue. Therefore, the council brought in as a consultant, Professor Richard M. Titmuss, of the London School of Economics. There was no one in this country intelligent enough to find out what is poverty and how to fight it in Canada! It was necessary to go outside the country to find someone who could show us what had to be done and how to do it.
Here is what the same Mr. Titmuss suggested:
Mr. Titmuss advised against a comprehensive study of poverty; instead, he recommended an extensive investigation on certain groups of low income families and individuals. He stated; "Proceed immediately by realistic stages like, for instance, the taking of photographs."

If the board appointed to study hardship had left its large, comfortable air-conditioned offices and taken the trouble of going down into the working class sections of our towns, into our villages and everywhere in the country, it would not have had to send for a Londoner to determine the extent of poverty in Canada. You can be sure that if it had sought hardship where it exists, in its actual surroundings, it would not have been long in finding solutions.

Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne delivered on April 5 included many items of varying importance, but it was not as allinclusive as some Members have claimed. There were significant omissions, and I propose to deal with one of the most important omissions briefly. I shall speak about the subject of the Canadian consumer and the complete absence of any mention of him in the Speech from the Throne.
First, just how important is the consumer in today's economy? At the present time the total value of goods and services produced in Canada is approximately $46 billion a year. Canadians have at their disposal for private spending about $27 billion a year. In addition to that they spend, through their Governments at all levels, several billion dollars a year. It is traditional to complain about taxes and Government spending, but I suggest that we may well receive better value for our money spent by Governments-in this sense I am speaking of Canadian citizens as public consumers-than we receive from our private spending or as individual consumers.
At least, at the level of Government, we have elected representatives who are in a position to scrutinize expenditures and bring the light of publicity on public spending. Further, it is generally true that Governments and other public bodies are sufficiently strong so that they have some power when they are making purchases for us. This is not so in our capacity as private consumers. In so many cases, it is the individual against the manufacturer or seller. Frequently, the contest is an unequal one, to say the least.
In the past, it was believed, according to conventional economic theory, that the consumer went into the marketplace to buy his goods and that sales and manufacturing were regulated by his choices. There was a companion doctrine which said: Let the buyer beware. I do not know if this ideal economic world ever existed, but it certainly does not exist today. It does not exist in this day of monopoly enterprise where a few giant firms can gang up on the consumer, not in this day when the extensive use of advertising and public relations techniques,

DEBATES	April 8, 1965
reinforced by the application of modern psychology, has tended to make the producer depend, not on the real qualities of his product but rather on the skills of advertising specialists to present a favourable impression of his goods; not in this day when producers are wary of price competition.
It is not difficult to enumerate many examples of the problems of the modern consumer. Any housewife knows examples of false and tricky packaging, and the difficulty of determining the price per ounce or per pound of a product. I speak of the soap manufacturer who markets a box of his product weighing one pound three and a half ounces for 41 cents; a two pound eight ounce package for 82 cents; and a four pound six and a half ounce package for $1.40. Then, there is the toothpaste which sells for 39 cents for a tube of 44 grams; 61 cents for 82 grams and 94 cents for 162 grams. Different manufacturers use different sizes of boxes and tubes so that the purchaser has a difficult time determining which is the best bargain. We simply don't have enough mathematicians in this country to accompany each housewife as she wends her way through the supermarkets, trying to determine the price per ounce or per pound.

I also wish to pay a tribute to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who retains and will always retain the firm confidence of all the members of our party. Our people are certainly fortunate in being led, through these trying times of a crucial importance for the future of our country, by a statesman who, apart from enjoying the confidence, the esteem and the admiration of the whole world, understood better than anyone else the problems which arose and are still arising at the national level.
Mr. Speaker, before discussing briefly certain proposals contained in the speech from the throne, I should like to refer to the area which I have the honour to represent in this parliament of the nation. The riding of Stan-stead is located in the heart of the eastern townships, one of the most picturesque regions in Canada and the third largest centre in the province, after Montreal and Quebec.
My riding is becoming increasingly urban although agriculture still plays an important part, while yielding to industrialization which should be given a new impetus by the recent improvements in the road system, the efficient operation of our industries, the leadership provided by our municipalities in making available industrial funds to facilitate the establishment of new industries, and also by the regional economic boards which can render tremendous services if they co-operate to carry out planned objectives.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, a problem is becoming more and more acute in my riding. The new activities continuously created are not adequate to meet the needs of our population and our region is losing through emigration, directly or indirectly, a good percentage of its population, especially members of the younger generation. The


problem of creating jobs for our young people is very difficult to solve, and I note with gratification that the government is fully conscious of the problem we are facing to facilitate the re-employment of workers displaced by automation or affected by other economic changes and that it intends to encourage regional development and contribute to the industrial development of regions that are not developing adequately.
The eastern townships constitute an industrial, agricultural and forest region.
Our chief industry, especially in the two main centres of my riding, namely the city of Magog and the town of Coaticook, is the textile industry and the area has developed in step with that basic industry. It employs about 35,000 people in the eastern townships and today it operates again at practically full capacity and its production can be estimated at about $500 million per year. That goes to show how important is that industry, and I am confident that the Canadian government will always keep in mind the protection of that industry whose future lies upon well defined tariffs and realistic trade policies rigidly enforced by government authorities, in order to protect that important industry which ranks first in many towns in the province and the country and which, too often, suffered as a result of international trade deficits.
Granite quarries, among the most important in the country, qualitatively as well as quantitatively, are also operated in my riding.
A prosperous agriculture, national forest management will remain for a long time to come the foundations of the economy of our region.

Doris Fleison writing in the Washington Star says, "It could just be that some well-meaning friend here decided to give Mr. Pearson a hand. Precisely that suggestion is going the rounds with a rather important name attached."
The second quotation was from the Chicago Sun Times and reads as follows:
The issue is political in Canada. The American press release seemed to correspond with the position of Diefenbaker's political opposition, Liberal Leader Lester Pearson.. .For our part we hope Washington hasn't committed a diplomatic Bay of Pigs with our friends the Canadians.
My third quotation was from Mr. Walter Lippmann, a very distinguished writer who commands a great deal of respect throughout the world. This is what he wrote:
American dealings with the Canadian Government have no doubt been complicated. But the crucial issue is the same one which has disrupted American relations with France and shaken the whole western alliance and has alienated the U.S. from General de Gaulle.

Adroit statecraft by the American State Department brought down the bungling, crypto-antiYankee Government of Prime Minister John Dief-enbaker and replaced it with a regime which promises to be faithful to the concept of Canadian-American interdependence.. .American intervention was coldly calculated to do precisely what it did, and it was a brilliant success.

Then, all of a sudden, to the amazement of most Americans, the United States found itself in an unseemly row with its indispensable close neighbour, Canada. The United States, through a misguided State Department press release, brought down the government of Prime Minister Diefen-baker.

I want to deal, Sir, with the so-called Butterwort'n letter, and put before the house the type of information which has been provided. The Prime Minister, as reported on page 322 of Hansard for May 27, came storming into the House to deliver himself of these profound remarks:
When this letter was brought to my attention, or a report of it, during the election campaign I let it be known then that I had received no such letter, and the United States ambassador let it be known that he had sent me no such letter.

My hon. friend opposite must have known that, and therefore the letter was a forgery; of course it was a forgery.

Two years later, there is uncertainty in the minds of members of this House and the people of this country with regard to some of the statements by the Prime Minister. On December 17 last year, 102 members of this House, in a recorded vote, expressed their uncertainty with regard to a statement made by the Prime Minister, an unprecedented

Thank you very much for reminding me of that. The Ambassador issued a statement, and I will put it on the record because I do not believe it has appeared on Hansard. No Member of the Government defended the Ambassador in this House. Here is what he published in the newspaper:
The alleged letter from me to the Prime Minister, the purported text of which I understand was read into the record of the House of Commons this afternoon, is a complete forgery. The forgery was brought to my attention during the recent election campaign.
I notified the then government that such a forgery was being circulated, and denied to enquirers who asked me about it at the time, that I had ever written any such letter. I reiterate the denial.
This is the sum and substance of the Ambassador's statement. There we are, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister said: I did not get the letter, it is a forgery. The Ambassador said: It is a complete forgery. Then the propaganda machinery of the Liberal party saw to it that I was condemned: I should not have raised this issue in the House of Commons. After all, the Prime Minister said if you do not get a letter, it is a forgery. He had not received this letter, and therefore I should not have read it in the House of Commons. So I was condemned all across the country for disclosing this information. There was an investigation instituted by the then Minister of Justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier. On July 15, Mr. Chevrier, in answer to a planted question, gave this reply as recorded at page 2182 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that It is the practice to make these reports public, but X can say rather summarily what the report did contain.
This is the R.C.M. Police report.
The investigation revealed first of all that there is no evidence that either of the two machines in use by the Ambassador's office at the embassy of the United States of America in Ottawa was used to execute any portion of the questioned typewriting.
There are just two machines, so a little foreign aid is required here. Perhaps they should have three or four. It does not say whether they were new machines or had been in use three or four months. I continue to quote:

Next, there is evidence to indicate that the paper comprising the covering letter and its envelope are products of an English firm. Finally, there is no evidence to indicate that the original of the photo copy was a composite or montage, but photographic techniques used in its preparation could obscure such evidence.
This was the result of the R.C.M. Police inquiry. What instructions did they get? What did they investigate? Were they called off? Did he finally decide it was an administrative matter which should be referred to the Postmaster General, because it was a letter and there might have been a stamp on it?
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
You will be interested to know that no question was asked me by the R.C.M.P.; no examination of the copy of the letter in my possession was ever carried out. The R.C.M.P., the Department of Justice, have no idea whether the copy in my possession is typed, or whether it is handwritten, or whether it is a photostat. They do not know whether it was mailed in New York or in Washington or in Ottawa; they do not know the country of origin of the paper upon which it appears. In short there was no investigation at all of the copy I admitted I had in my possession-no investigation at all. It is somewhat strange that the then Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) did not consider it necessary to have an investigation made.
I have reported what was said by the Prime Minister and by two Ministers of the Crown as well as by the Ambassador. I have disclosed, as did the Minister of Justice, the abortive and incomplete investigation carried out by the R.C.M.P. When you have as little information as this, you must refer to the press.
I examined rather carefully as many of the press stories as came to my notice, and I discovered that some of the gentlemen of the fourth estate had a little more information than was given by Mr. Chevrier or by the Mounted Police. I cannot refer to all of them but I do not think Mr. Blakely would object if I were to refer to his account in the Montreal Gazette on May 29. I quote:
Informants say one flaw in the document was that in assembling the photographic stages the physical proportions of letterhead, type and signature were thrown out. The photostat, reproduced to the normal size of U.S. Embassy notepaper, would have the document's text running off the normal-sized page.
This was new and important information. In the Star Weekly magazine of October 26 a feature article by Don Peacock appeared,
April 8, 1965

and in the course of that article he had this to say:
But the giveaway was all in the body of the letter. Aside from the atrocious writing style, the contents were too long to fit on an actual-size-sheet of the embassy stationery of which the photostat purported to be a reduced copy.
By typing out the letter with the same line lengths, spacings and margins as were used in the photostat, embassy officials found the stationery about five lines too short.
Then, further on, he said:
The Mounties made the same typing test with the purported stationery as the embassy had and with the same result that the officials obtained: The "letter" was too long for the paper.
May I just summarize the so-called evidence at this point? There is the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who simply said the letter was a forgery. There was the statement of the Prime Minister that he had not received such a letter and that therefore, of course, it was a forgery. There was the Ambassador's statement that he did not write the letter, and then the evidence which the press obtained from informants that the letter when typed out on normal sized stationery ran over the page.
How conclusive is this evidence? May I suggest to people who are interested in investigating this matter at this late date that they should try doing two or three things. First they might type the letter on paper measuring eight and a half by twelve and a half inches. They will find that it fits. I had this done. It occurred to me that perhaps the letter had been written on stationery larger than the article which I have quoted called normal size. I have known for a number of years that there are several sizes of stationery used in offices-eight and a half inches by nine inches, eight inches by ten inches, eight and a half inches by eleven inches-and eight and a half inches by twelve and a half inches. Type out the letter on a sheet measuring eight and a half inches by twelve and a half inches and you will find that it fits perfectly.
Then I would suggest to an investigator that he take a photostat of the letter written on a sheet of paper of those dimensions and reduce it to the size of four and a half inches by seven and a half inches. He will find he has a photostat which corresponds to the photostat which was printed in some of the newspapers-the same size and the same spacing.

Then I suggest that if anyone is interested he might ask the United States Embassy to give him a sample of the embassy stationery measuring eight and a half inches by twelve and a half inches with the seal of the United States in the upper lefthand corner and the words "Embassy of the United States of America" embossed in the upper righthand corner. If they have not used it up by now they may have some left over from 1962-63. An investigator might also want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether by any chance there has been any correspondence with his office over the years in the course of which stationery measuring eight and a half inches by twelve and a half inches was used by the United States Ambassador.
I took one of these elementary steps and I found that the letter did not run off the page. So what credence can one place in these stories from informants or from the Mounties-if that is accurate-that the letter must obviously be a forgery because it is greater than the size of the normal stationery? The Grit propaganda machine got working on this at full blast and I was subjected to editorial comment and attention in various articles, all because the Prime Minister said the letter had not been received and that therefore, of course it was a forgery, and because informants said that when typed out it ran over the page. I do not know how long evidence of that kind would stand up in a court of law.
There are some interesting questions which could be asked, and I wish the Prime Minister would clear them up. After all, he raised this issue; he re-opened it. I ask him this: If the letter was a forgery, why would a letter dated January 14 not become available in January, February or March if it was intended for use in the election campaign? I ask a second question: was the letter ever intended to be sent to the Prime Minister or was it a useful document for fund-raising if shown to the right people at the right time, indicating powerful support for the Liberals? I ask a third question: Perhaps the Ambassador had nothing to do with it. He issued a statement, but no Member of the Government defended him here in the House of Commons.
Far be it from me to question anything that an Ambassador states or writes but I note on looking carefully at his statement that he simply says: "It is a complete forgery. I deny that I have ever written any such

I am not questioning the Ambassador's statement but in similar circumstances I would have said: "I have never written such a letter; and I have never dictated such a letter; such a letter has never been produced by my secretarial staff and I have never signed such a letter." That is the type of statement I would have issued in those circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, as is customary, the debate currently taking place is covering a wide range of local, regional, national and international problems. The Speech from the Throne itself sets the stage for such a broad discussion. Although it is traditional that very few details of proposed legislation are indicated in


the Speech, I think this one is so general in nature that it is very difficult to know just what may be forthcoming. However, as we look over the Speech from the Throne we find that there are a great many items of real interest, and I believe that in one sense it does indicate that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Government is interested in the development of human resources, as is indicated in the Speech.
Throughout the various debates that are held in this House we find constant reference to the need to conserve and develop our natural resources, and I believe this is very Important. Too many times we have found that criminal waste has taken place as far as natural resources are concerned. We have had to face the alternative of revising our legislation, revising our concept of the problem, or else facing the inevitable consequences of our neglect. However, if it is wrong *-and I am sure we all agree that it is-to neglect the proper conservation and development of natural resources, then I believe it is doubly criminal if we are to in any way fail to develop and conserve our human resources. This would be, I believe, the repudiation of the basic principle of democracy.
Someone has said that it is every person's desire to be somebody, to be recognized as an individual and to make a contribution to the age in which he lives. I believe this is basically true. However there are certain things that somehow or other tend to minimize the importance of the individual. I suppose that the very magnitude of the universe in which we live and the fact that so many of its vast secrets are being revealed to man today somehow tend to dwarf the individual. Then we think of the society in which we find ourselves, in which we are pretty well classed, not as individuals with a name but as a unit with a number. This, perhaps, also tends to submerge the individual in the mass of mankind. But in spite of this I believe that the individual, his needs, his aspirations, his capabilities, his welfare must be the paramount concern of those who occupy places of responsibility and leadership.
Therefore I would say that one of the basic principles of our democratic society must be that the individual be assisted to achieve a full and abundant life through the exercise of personal initiative and the assumption of individual responsibility. Every person must have a constitutional right to live his own life, make his own decisions, develop his own personality and pursue his own activities,
April 8, 1965

provided that in so doing he does not infringe upon the similar rights of others. I would like to think that this document which we have before us today in the form of the Speech from the Throne is a recognition of this fact and expresses the desire and the determination of the Government to do something worth while in assisting in creating the kind of economy and the kind of society that will enable the individual citizens of Canada to achieve their true greatness as individuals and not just as a unit of a larger organization. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I just wanted to make reference to that particular aspect of the Speech before I enter into some of the more specific recommendations and specific proposals that have been made.
There is one that perhaps fits in very closely with this idea of the development of human resources and the development of human personality. That is the reference in the Speech from the Throne to the desire of the Government to establish new legislation as far as our Indian people are concerned. I know this has to do mainly with material things, but it does recognize the fundamental rights of the Indian people of this country. I refer to the Indian Claims Commission that is to be set up. Now, Mr. Speaker, I realize that the need for such a Commission has been constantly urged upon the Government; it has been urged by representatives of the Indian people themselves, by organizations that are concerned with the welfare of these citizens of Canada, and also individuals who on their own have given some thought and consideration to the problems that these people are facing.
In 1963 a bill was introduced in the House, Bill C-130; it was introduced for first reading on December 14, 1963. The purpose of this measure was to try to undo some of the injustices that had been perpetrated in days gone by. But unfortunately we did not get very far with that particular measure, or with many other measures for that matter, and now we find that once again the Government has indicated in the Speech from the Throne that they will be introducing a bill to establish an Indian Claims Commission. Following the introduction of Bill C-130 a great deal of study went into that particular document, and at conferences of Indian people that were held across the country a great deal of consideration was given to the various clauses. It was felt that if this was to really be effective in solving these problems and in dispensing justice to the
The Address-Mr. Patterson Indian people, a great many amendments would have to be made. These were submitted to the Government as well as to various Members of Parliament-I suppose, to all Members of Parliament-and I trust that in the drafting of the new legislation the Government will take into consideration the briefs that were presented by the Indian people themselves and by other interested organizations, and will see to it that the very best possible piece of legislation will be introduced with a view to meeting the requirements of and solving the problems in this particular connection.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I believe there is a new conscience being developed with respect to the needs of our Indian peoples. We must recognize their aspirations, we must recognize their abilities and we must recognize their rights. If we are to fulfil our responsibility and recognize the basic principle that all men are equal, then I believe we must do something definite and positive to meet the needs and to solve some of these problems which have been of such concern to the Indian people down through the past years.
There is one matter to which I should like to refer which is not included in the Speech from the Throne, although perhaps it is in some indirect manner. I refer once again to the problems we are facing in my own constituency with respect to the Fraser River. On February 28, 1964 I dealt with the recommendations of the interim report of the Fraser River Board and urged action. I should like to refer briefly to what I said in Hansard on that occasion, as reported at page 381:
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have this problem outlined for us. The board introduced an interim report in 1956 which contained specific recommendations which it felt were necessary and advisable at that time. The thing that concerns the people of the lower Fraser Valley at the moment is that in spite of the fact specific recommendations were made nothing has been done up to this time. We have been advised that the final report of the board will be brought in some time this spring, possibly in March. It is our hope and expectation that as soon as this report is introduced the governments concerned, both provincial and federal, will give immediate attention to it and will endeavour to work out a satisfactory solution to these problems.
As I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that statement was made on February 28, 1964. The final report was prepared and tabled in the month of March. The question I should like to ask at this time is: Just how much progress has been made up to the present in carrying
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Patterson out the recommendations of the Fraser River Board? I recognize the fact that considerable study would have to be put into the problem. Engineering studies and all these other things would no doubt take time. But one year later we still face the situation where nothing tangible or concrete has been done to meet and to solve the problems in that particular field.
Last Spring saw the danger point reached once again. There was great fear in the minds of the people in the area that once again they would be faced with, perhaps, a repetition of the flood of 1948. The farmers of this area suffer heavily from seepage through the dikes. At one place there was a break in the dikes. We are now moving toward that time of the year when once again we face the possibility of a recurrence of this situation. As I have pointed out, apparently nothing concrete has been done up to the present to attempt to eliminate the possibility of this situation developing once again.
