Mr. Speaker, I recognize the fact that these matters to which the Minister has referred have come about, but I would say with regard to that one particular problem, the matter of the dikes, that it did take a very long time to receive a reply and for something concrete to be done. I was speaking to the municipal authorities and they were very concerned. They said that if they were going to meet the problem and repair and strengthen the dikes so that they would not be faced with the same situation again, the Government would really have to

get cracking. I appreciate the fact that this agreement has been worked out, but I am not laying the blame altogether on the Federal Government. However, I would say once again, on behalf of the people of that particular area who face the danger of flooding, that we would expect both Provincial and Federal Governments to act with dispatch in solving this problem and bringing relief to this particular situation.
I should now like to deal with another problem, which is the main problem to which I should like to make reference today. I refer to the allusions in the Speech from the Throne to agriculture. There seems to be quite a section of the Speech from the Throne devoted to agriculture legislation. Part of the Speech reads as follows:
My Government is developing new policies to enable farmers generally to achieve larger and more reliable incomes so that their living and working standards will be comparable to those enjoyed in other sectors of our economy.
This is setting out, I believe, the main objective in the mind of the Government regarding agriculture and agricultural problems.
If we look back to the last Speech from the Throne we find that reference is made to agriculture and some proposed legislation. But no matter how much pressure was put upon the Government and no matter how many recommendations were made, it did not seem as though we got around to considering the agricultural problems as such. Therefore, I hope that the measures forecast in the field of agriculture in this Speech will receive better treatment from the Government than did those included in the Throne Speech of last year. These references are very general. There is no indication just what specific measures will be taken or recommended, but we will await the details with a great deal of interest.
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, agriculture remains an industry basic to our whole economy. No matter how much industrialization takes place and no matter how much development in secondary industries takes place, agriculture remains the basic industry of this great nation of ours. In the carrying out of the activities in this particular area, our people face a great variety of problems; but it just seems as though the farmers cannot forecast or anticipate them.
They never know just which ones they will have to face from year to year. I think of my own constituency in the Fraser Valley, and of others which are facing the same problems.
April 8, 1965

Last fall once again the fruit growers faced a very heavy frost which destroyed a great portion of the strawberry plants.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
They have been trying to figure out ways and means of reestablishing or rehabilitating the industry. They have made representations to the Provincial Government and have been successful in obtaining some assistance, but when one thinks of the assistance given to the agricultural industry in various parts of Canada by the Federal Government it seems that there should be some way in which these people can be assisted by the Federal Government, as well as by Provincial authorities. This is just one of the difficult and uncertain problems which faces the agricultural industry across this nation today.
In addition to those problems, Canadians in the agricultural industry today must face the difficulties created by a general increase in the cost of production and a decrease in net income. This problem has never been solved. It has been discussed and studied from many angles, but to the present date no solution has been found. I hope that the Government in fulfilling its promises contained in the Speech from the Throne will be able to come up with some worth-while solutions to this problem.
At this time I should like to refer to several measures referred to in the Speech from the Throne. It contains a forecast of an expanded program in respect of agricultural manpower. Such a program has been referred to in the past, and suggestions relating to this very serious problem, which exists in many parts of the country have been made. Agricultural organizations have referred to it in briefs presented to various authorities. The Government has shown some wisdom by giving attention to this difficult situation at this time.
I should like to read a statement made at page 18 of a brief presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In that brief this is stated:
On this question of availability of seasonal labour particularly we suggest that a special study group be set up, on which there would be representatives of the Canadian Horticultural Council as well as other Federation representatives, plus representatives of appropriate Government departments. It should be the job of such a study group to thoroughly assess the situation and the problem, and attempt to work out policies which can be effectively applied to prevent recurrence of the difficulties experienced in the past year.
No doubt the Government has given some attention to the recommendations of various
The Address-Mr. Patterson agricultural organizations and, as I pointed out earlier, we will look forward with interest to the introduction of legislation which will assist in solving this problem.
Another reference in the Throne Speech to the agricultural industry is the suggestion that the Government is going to introduce policies which will achieve larger and more reliable incomes. I suppose this means that the Government intends to introduce legislation designed to bring a fair share of the national income to the agricultural industry. This is something we have urged upon various governments over the years. Representatives of every party in this House have urged this upon the Government, and I am sure that Members of all parties in this House have given thought to recommendations in respect of increasing and stabilizing farm incomes. Such an accomplishment would provide farmers with a better opportunity for budgeting their money to meet their financial obligations from year to year.
The arguments I have advanced in regard to the agricultural industry in general can be specifically applied to the poultry industry, the dairy industry, the small fruits industry and to all these various segments of the agricultural industry which must face these problems. These industries are all looking for help and guidance which will enable them to increase and balance their incomes, so that they may face the future with the knowledge that they can count on a certain income each year.
One other paragraph of the Throne Speech is related specifically to the dairy industry and the establishment of a Canadian Dairy Commission. It is my opinion that it is essential to establish such a body, Mr. Speaker, and in this regard I should like to refer to an article which appeared in one of the newspapers published in my area of the country, the Abbotsford Sumas and Matsqui News, which is a very reputable newspaper as are all the newspapers in that area. This article refers to the problems which the dairy industry faces, and it concludes with the following words:
Mr. Brannick, President of the FVMPA, put It in a nutshell at the annual meeting last week.
"Prices must be increased to the Canadian farmer, or Canada will become an importing nation." He added "this is unthinkable."
With reference to the dairy industry particularly, and to the whole agricultural industry in general, it will be a sad day indeed when farmers reach that point, which many
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Patterson of them have already reached, where they are not able to carry on and must go out of business, forcing Canada to become an importing country in respect of agricultural produce. At such time we will be left at the mercy of other agricultural producing countries, as far as prices are concerned.
The Throne Speech referred also to the movement of feed grain, and suggested the establishment of an organization or agency to deal with this particular problem as it affects Eastern Canada and British Columbia. In the old days when I first came to Ottawa one of our main themes in this House related to this feed grain situation. We urged the Government to adopt a program for providing assistance in respect of the movement of feed grain.
This situation is still critical, and particularly so in British Columbia where the industry is facing competition from industry in other areas which have access to cheaper feed. In that area the people are forced to pay high prices for feed grain, and find that the difficulties created as a result of these high prices are greater than they can surmount. We hope that the Government, in working out a solution to this problem, will be able to develop something which will be fair to every part of Canada, and which will give producers in all areas an equal opportunity to share in the benefits resulting from any policy adopted.
The Throne Speech suggests that the Government is interested in the maintenance of the family farm structure in Canada. Agricultural organizations across Canada have been concerned in this regard for many years and have advocated a program of assistance for the maintenance of family farm units. There has been a trend toward the development of larger farm units and the integration of small farms into large agricultural operations. These agricultural organizations have been concerned about this trend because of the possibility that small family farm units will become things of the past. As I have pointed out in the past on many occasions, individuals who operate small family farms do not do so only to make a living for themselves and their families, but because this is a way of life which they enjoy and want to maintain. They have no desire to move into the city and become units of a Canadian industrial labour force. Farming, to these individuals, is a way of life which they enjoy, and one which they wish to perpetuate. These farmers only want

a fair opportunity to live with decency and dignity, and with incomes which are sufficient to enable them to meet the needs of their families. Therefore I would urge the Government to encourage the Department of Agriculture to concern itself with this situation. I believe that family farm units are an essential part of the general economy of this country.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I want to refer to a statement regarding this matter in the submission by the National Farmers Union to the Government of Canada on March 1, 1965. On page 7 they say:
If the farm family is to be the keystone of national agricultural policy, this can be achieved through the implementation of farm policies which make it economically possible for the farmer to maintain his family and himself with a sense of dignity and at the same time apply sound farming practices to his land.
There are many other matters to which consideration could be given this afternoon but I wanted to refer particularly to some of the problems related to the agricultural industry. I wish to commend the Government for facing some of these problems and I hope they will be able to come up with an answer that will be satisfactory to the industry itself, and will be of benefit to the economy of our great country. As I have said, there are many subjects I should like to cover but time does not permit. Others of my colleagues will be dealing with various matters of importance and concern, and I appreciate this opportunity to call to the attention of the Government some of these problems of urgent concern.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must extend my heartfelt congratulations to the mover, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), and the seconder, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. If I may, I should like to single out the member for the constituency next to mine for the manner in which he represented the St. Maurice valley.
The session just ended was a long and hard one, but it achieved most gratifying results for this country, since we were able to move ahead in the program we had set for ourselves and that we had placed before the people during the 1963 election campaign.
I am glad to see also that the speech from the throne provides for a reform of parliamentary procedure. I can only hope that the
April 8. 1965

new procedure will do away with the endless repetition of the same arguments and the same speeches, as was the case during the last session.
Why not set a time limit on debates as is done for the speech from the throne debate and allow the tabling of other speeches as having been read, even if there should be a day of discussion where party leaders or their spokesmen would state their policy which, I think, would waste less time while offering the same result and respecting the democratic process.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Champlain which I represent-I like to repeat it-is one of the privileged ridings in the province of Quebec. After a survey, it was found that nobody wants to see it broken up under the new redistribution. That riding, located between Montreal and Quebec, is adjacent to the ridings of Three Rivers, St. Maurice-Lafleche and Portneuf.
My riding is both rural and urban. Cap de la Madeleine, an industrial city, has a population of almost 30,000 and the rest of the riding is divided into 19 rural communities, typical of French Canada, without forgetting my own native village of St. Tite.
It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that I should often ask for retaining walls, wharves and marinas, since a part of my riding is along the St. Lawrence River, from Cap de la Madeleine to Champlain, Batiscan, Ste Anne de la Perade-the kingdom of tommy cods- with Ste Genevieve de Batiscan.
The city of Cap de la Madeleine is known throughout the world for its sanctuary which attracts thousands of people every year. "The Cape", as it is called, is an industrial city in the highest sense of the word and an ideal site, like all communities in my riding, to set up prosperous industries. We have a healthy and hard-working population.
The establishment of a steel mill in Becan-cour was greeted with much enthusiasm in my constituency because it will have economic repercussions throughout my area.
Becancour stands opposite St. Marthe du Cap de la Madeleine. Its fabulous development will no doubt provide a most sound argument for speeding up the extension of the Three Rivers harbour toward Cap de la Madeleine, for which we have been clamouring for a long time.
While Cap de la Madeleine has developed at a rapid pace and has a bright future, each parish in my riding would like to expand,
The Address-Mr. Matte and rightly so, and they are all opened to industry. I am looking forward to the day when each municipality will be able to live comfortably from the proceeds of industry and farming, as much from one source as from the other.
Farmers make up an important section of our population. They suffer, as all eastern farmers, from an unpropitious situation. The new dairy policy of this government will no doubt give hope to those people who, more than any other, need to be looked after. Under section 95 of our constitution, farming must come under the joint jurisdiction of Ottawa and the provinces.
I am proud to say that the speech from the throne will bring a ray of hope to the honest and good people who, let us not forget it, are the descendants of the founders of our country. In fact, it provides for:
1.	Measures to help farmers increase their income and assistance to rural families;
2.	The establishment of a Canadian dairy commission;
3.	Improved movement and marketing of feed grain in eastern Canada and British Columbia;
4.	Creation of a fund for rural economic development and amendments to ARDA, the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act.
What a gratifying program when we see the sincerity the present government brings into its fight against poverty, which should not exist in our fine country.
1.	Parliament will be called upon to grant the Prime Minister the necessary powers to administer a program to fight poverty.
2.	A commission will study the opportunity of creating a position of ombudsman, a sort of protector of the people.
3.	The program of assistance to underdeveloped districts will be extended.
4.	The creation of a system of assistance at the federal level, and many other measures to assist the people according to the concepts of co-operative federalism.
Mr. Speaker, my riding has known unemployment too often, and that is the worse plague which can exist. Employment is a source of happiness for everyone, and unemployment is a real calamity. I am fully conscious of this situation as a result of the many visits I receive from unemployed persons in my office.
Every man has a right to work, especially in a country like Canada, and it is our duty
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Matte to look particularly alter those who suffer, as the speech from the throne states so rightly.
This brings me to deal with unemployment insurance which will be improved by the government. I find the word unemployment a pejorative and I would like that fund to be called "Worker compensation fund", which I feel is more positive.
Why could unemployment insurance benefits, a social measure, not be paid to a worker who falls ill but who must nevertheless support his family? And yet, if a recipient falls ill at such times, he continues to draw benefits.
The reforms will no doubt remove all those anomalies.
I would also like the department to be more human and to apply simpler regulations to the people. I often think it is unfair for some people to be able to evade the law while others, through ignorance, are being refused benefits.
During the 1963 federal election, we submitted a five-point plan as follows: (1) revive the economy of Canada; (2) restore security; (3) preserve confederation; (4) develop the agricultural industry; (5) restore Canada's prestige.
Mr. Speaker, considering the accomplishments we have witnessed until now and this speech from the throne, we can formally declare that we kept our promises to the people, for after two years only, all those planks of our platform have been implemented. There is still much to be done, we are aware of the facts and we are being consistent.
I have received several delegations from my riding and I take this opportunity to thank the protective staff and the staff of the house for their courtesy and willingness to help visitors. However, I wonder if it would not be a good idea to put bilingual people at the main entrances because quite often people who can speak both official languages are relegated where such knowledge is not as necessary.
Before closing, I would like to pay tribute to our great Prime Minister who, more than any other man, has really understood the problem of unity, and I truly believe that he was the man chosen by Divine Providence to save Canada.
He knows how to engage in dialogue; he is the man of peace, that peace he personifies and spreads around him in our country and throughout the world. We are all the more

convinced of that in view of the award he received recently from the University of Philadelphia.
Mr. Speaker, "a flame of ideals is burning in the heart of our fine youth", said the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche, a flame is burning in the hearts of all the citizens in my province. I hope I will see the day-not far away, I hope-when all together, throughout the country, equally, in complete unity and conscious of our diversity, we can sing whole heartedly and fully convinced "O Canada, beloved country of mine".

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the start to compliment the previous speakers on their presentations relating to the Speech from the Throne. My only comment on the Throne Speech is that it is a truly fantastic play on words. In order to describe the verbiage contained therein, I should like to recall an old Irish saying in our family which goes like this: Talk is cheap, but it takes money to buy whiskey. I do not believe there is any segment of the population that has not been mentioned in a general way for health or welfare. There is even a plan for those unfortunate Canadians who are in jail. Of course it is obvious that neither Lucien Rivard nor Hal Banks will be able to benefit, as things stand at the moment.
The announcement in the Speech from the Throne that Parliament is finally going to have an opportunity to discuss the agreement with the United States covering the automobile industry is indeed most welcome. It is long overdue. This agreement, which appears to be as one-sided as anything ever entered into by the Canadian Government, affects a wide range of industries in Canada. It affects

the livelihood of many Canadians, and many of them are In my own constituency. These people want to know, what is this agreement and how was it made? How will it operate in the future? speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock I had commented on the lack of information given to Parliament concerning the mechanics of the free trade car deal with the United States.
There are many questions that come to mind. What kind of deal is it which gives the big automobile companies a debate of $50 million in exise duties they would otherwise pay on parts imported into Canada, while
DEBATES	143
The Address-Mr. McCutcheon not one consumer in Canada gets one cent of advantage out of it? We are told to have faith and put our trust in the Government because everything will work out well. We are told there will be a tremendous growth in employment; that the companies need this extra money for a few years for development purposes. The question which comes to my mind is this: If this deal is so good why are the ordinary investment channels not available to Canadian manufacturers for expansion? In this way the benefit of the excise rebate could be passed back to the consumers, the car buying public. Of course we have been given the promise that cars will be cheaper in price. But when? And by how much?
Blame for lack of information about this plan, and failure to understand it, lies on the shoulders of the Government as a whole, but particularly upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). They go down to the United States, sit around a table with the United States administration and come back and tell us that all will be well if only Canada will cut down its tariff on United States automobile parts. On some bright, sunny day in the future, they tell us, the Americans may cut down their tariffs and let Canadian cars into the United States duty free. They tell us that the President cannot carry out this bargain until the Congress of of the United States decides whether or not to lower automobile tariffs. That is perfectly true. It is Congress which will eventually decide. The President of the United States proposes and Congress disposes. This is the principle of United States policy that Canadians have learned the hard way in the past. I do not think we should have to learn it the hard way in every generation.
Already there are signs that there will be opposition to such a move in the United States Congress. As a consequence we are in the hands of one man. Our auto deal depends on whether or not the President's popularity and his salesmanship of his ideas can effectively force this measure through the Congress.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
One fact has been overlooked, however. It is that the President already possesses some power to cut tariffs. Indeed he can cut them up to 50 per cent for bargaining purposes. Did the Prime Minister ask for a cut to be made in Canada's favour? We do
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. McCutcheon not know. Did the Secretary of State for External Affairs remind the Right Hon. Gentleman that President Johnson could have cut the United States tariff in our favour, had he so wished, without waiting for the approval of Congress? We do not know. Did the Minister of Industry jog his colleague's elbow and urge him to ask the President to make tariff concessions which might save a few thousand Canadian industrial jobs? We need 1J million more jobs in Canada in the next few years, as the Economic Council has pointed out. I do not think we want agreements with foreign countries that cut down jobs in Canada; and I can tell this House that a lot of people are saying in my part of the country that the Liberal Government has lost its shirt in making this automobile deal with President Johnson. It is not the Government's shirt; it is the shirt of some small Canadian manufacturers of automobile parts and accessories. Do you think we are going to get our shirt back? Well, we are merely told to wait and see.
I mentioned previously that the future of this automobile deal depends on one man. This concerns me very much, because it reminds me of some of the things I learned on a recent trip down into the United States. I visited in Texas; in fact, I visited at the L. B. J. Ranch, not far from Austin. They get a lot of visitors down there these days. I would like to comment, in passing, that I can recommend a visit to Texas for my friends and colleagues in the House of Commons. It's a great state, and Texans are a great people. In our part of the country we see lots of Texans visiting Canada, and we like them. I submit that it would be a change for our Government if some of the Ministers got in their cars, as I did, and drove down. They then would find out what ordinary Americans think about this Government and some of the things it is doing. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) goes to places like Hyannis Port, Philadelphia and Camp David. He has lunch with the President; he makes speeches, and he has his newspaper clippings about them. This is not the same as talking to the man in the street in places like Houston, Austin and Tyler. This is what is called the grass roots approach, I am told. One thing about Texas, when I was there in January, is that while it is a beautiful country-and they have lots of beautiful country-they have also plenty of dry, stony and rough country; and it looks particularly rough and dry and stony to anyone who

comes from Ontario, the garden land of North America-

-the riding that I happen to represent, which embraces Lambton and Kent Counties. The L. B. J. Ranch is in the Pedernales country; and I must give credit to anyone who has made a ranch and a home in that rough country of rock and sagebrush. The President has a nice little lake right on the ranch. They have built a dam across the river; and there is also a nice big airstrip to take the biggest, fastest jet aircraft, so he can go to and come from Washington. Those Texans down there know Lyndon Johnson, and it is interesting for a Canadian to get the Texas point of view.
I would like to report what I heard in Johnson City, Texas, which is 11 miles away from the L. B. J. Ranch. It is a thriving place and has a population of 611. I visited with farmers and ranchers who came into the town the day I was there. I talked with them in the casual, friendly way that they have in Texas, and this one man in particular had a word of advice which I am going to pass on to the Prime Minister of Canada. We talked about Texas and the United States, and we got into discussion about this automobile agreement. I said to him, "What do you think about this car deal between the President and our Prime Minister?" I had hoped the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) would be here, because he could take some notes on real diplomacy as this Texan spelled it out to me. "Well", said this man from Johnson City, in his Texas drawl, "I reckon your Prime Minister better have his shirt well buttoned down, 'cos if'n he ain't, I can tell you who is going to have that shirt pretty soon; it's going to be our Lyndon". He went on, "You know, our Lyndon is one of the biggest wheeler-dealers in Texas, and if'n your Prime Minister don't have his underwear on tight, he may lose that, too". Well, I guess he could see that I, as a Canadian, did not like the idea of our Prime Minister losing his shirt and underwear to L. B. J., even in the cause of cementing the long friendship between Canada and the United States; so he added these words, "Of course, our Lyndon is a real Texas gentleman, and he will lend your Prime Minister his shirt back so he can get home safe".
April 8. 1965

Mr. Speaker, I am not worried today about the Prime Minister and his shirt; I am concerned about his image abroad. The Prime Minister may be the dove of peace in Philadelphia, but I suspect he is just a pigeon in Texas. I can tell this House that a great many Canadians in the small parts manufacturing companies around Ontario are worried about losing their shirts; and the sooner Parliament gets down to examining this automobile agreement and hearing directly from the Minister of Industry, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister the exact terms they have agreed to, then the better it will be for Canada.
I noticed in the London Free Press recently an article which was headed up, "Ford Exporting 400 Cars Monthly to New York State". It goes on to say that Ford of Canada has started exporting 400 cars a month to dealers in Upper New York State, the first time the company has shipped to the United States. This is datelined Oakville, Ontario. The question that comes to my mind is this: How can Ford Motor Company export cars to the United States of America and pay 84 per cent duty to the United States Government, and still be competitive? I am sure that our American cousins are not going to pay any more for these cars manufactured at Oakville than they will pay for domestic models manufactured in the United States of America. I confess that I do not have the answer, but I can only surmise that Ford must be discounting their price at least 8i per cent in order to be competitive. The question in my mind is this: If they can do it for Americans, why can't they do it for Canadians?
War on poverty is a fine, abstract doctrine, even if this is borrowed, like a shirt, from President Johnson. What we want to avoid in this country is importing poverty from the United States. Unless the automobile agreement starts working, and working pretty soon, in Canada's favour, that is exactly what the Prime Minister is doing; he is importing poverty for the employees in the production of automobile parts. So I have this to offer to the Government: You have no monopoly on knowledge of all the things that are good for Canada. Take us into your confidence some time; you might be pleasantly surprised to learn that we are as interested as anyone in Canada's welfare. After all, you should thank the Opposition for correcting a lot of your ill-conceived legislation.
The Address-Mr. Latulippe

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like all other hon. members,
I should like to express my thanks to the mover, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and also to offer them my sincere congratulations for having carried out their responsibility so well.
In the Speech from the Throne read by His Excellency the Governor General, it should be noted that a very definite emphasis is put on economic and social problems.
The government intends to fight poverty and unemployment, improve the protection provided for Canadians against the dangers of illness, facilitate the adaptation of workers to new requirements of technology, stimulate the development of underdeveloped regions. All those are initiatives that will meet very real needs in this country.
Finally, the Speech from the Throne refers to the delicate matter of jurisdiction between Ottawa and the provinces.
The Government is only realizing now that there is dissatisfaction everywhere, hardship and poverty. Poverty has been deliberately maintained by the old-line parties, especially the Liberal Party which has been in office for 33 out of 45 years. We now have to resort to mobilization to fight poverty. What have old governments done to date to establish a debt free monetary system based on present and potential production? What are both Liberal and Conservative parties doing to provide, out of our colossal production, the necessities of life to everyone? Have they passed any legislation to protect the large family, the farmer or the settler? They all have a hard time to make both ends meet.
Under the old-line parties there is nothing but poverty, unpaid debts, mortgages, mortgaged governments and subservient people forever in debt to a few Canadian financial institutions and, in a proportion of 80 per cent, to foreign interests. To remedy this situation, instead of distributing our abundant available production, the old-line parties and especially the Liberal Party are becoming leftists in accepting state socialism, which is contrary to individual freedom, and they presented it to us as a remedy in proposing a series of measures aimed at correcting a situation which has become unbearable when
April 8. 1965

The Address-Mr. Latulippe they should be putting an end to that situation; they use it as a starting point; they put the blame on private industry and try to replace it. This is probably a part of a great scheme to establish a super universal state.
The strategy of the secret force calling the shots is very simple but effective: first, create unbearable conditions; second, state interference, with economic improvements paid through the loss of certain freedoms. There is the occult power which acts as a financial system to put private enterprise in a difficult position and which liberates the same financial system at the right time on behalf of public enterprise to make it look good.
It must be remembered that man is not born to produce, that life should not be spent exclusively on producing material goods. Economic security is necessary if freedom is to mean something, but once a minimum of economic security is guaranteed, freedom becomes much more important than wealth.
Under normal circumstances modern production is already more than enough to offer good living conditions to all. Why then all those programs for employment and large scale production with the intervention of the state, everywhere private enterprise cannot keep everyone at work? What is the purpose of all that when there is enough for the necessities of life for some extra comforts too? Why not leave alone those who are satisfied with such necessities of life, such comforts.
For those who are interested solely in material objectives, the employment and production plans may have a meaning for those who want a socialist state; they may have a meaning for the enlightened people from the London School of Economics, from this seminary for the training of the higher bureaucrats of the socialist state of tomorrow.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
But they do not make sense for those who, like the Creditistes, have a broader concept of the human person, and they are distasteful to those who refuse to give up freedom for materialism. What every individual should acknowledge as the main purpose of economic activity should be to free man while providing everyone with his vital needs.
It is then that freedom makes sense and that it is odious to allow it to take a back seat it to the requirements of planners.
For instance, our fine pension plan which brings the human being into subjection, is one of the most socialistic measures ever enacted in Canada.

I urge all right-minded people to join with those who suggest the English and French Canadians are able to solve their own problems and that since production has been organized for a long time, it should be easy to ensure its distribution. Our two old line parties have at last generally admitted that there is something completely wrong with our economic system and that it is also absurd to refuse to men devoid of the necessities of life the necessary money to obtain them, simply because there is such an overabundance of those things and that no labour is required for further production.
The factor limiting production of actual wealth has been the failure to distribute products, because the consumer does not have the money required to buy everything.
Production is short-lived, Mr. Speaker, when there is no buyer. Mass production requires mass consumption. It is therefore necessary to investigate the purchasing power mechanism in order to meet the needs.
And, while a surprising evolution took place in the science of production, no similar change occurred in the financial machinery. The system of distribution of the purchasing power dates back to centuries of scarcity when there were insufficient goods to meet the needs of the people.
There should be an end to worries, to unjust orders issued to protect some friends at the expense of other people. There should be an end to requests for privileges; now it is the people's turn to live.
The citizens want their freedom and I think that sooner or later there will be a freedom march of the Canadian citizens.
Governments have always found money to wage war or arrange for international massacres. They have always found a means to finance their war budgets. The budget and the economy were balanced in wartime. Natural resources and productivity were successfully mobilized. The necessary capital was always found to wage war. Nothing was impossible for the sake of war. What we did to win the war, let us do it now for the sake of peace. What was spent for guns, let us spend for our fellow citizens, our children and ourselves.
Let us now accelerate our production and our productivity and let us put all these goods at the disposal of our fellow citizens. Let us help our poverty stricken families. Let us put an end to poverty and indigence. Let us put an end to ignorance, incompetence and unemployment. Let us put all our adults
April 8, 1965

to work; it is done in other countries. Would we be incompetent, mentally retarded, careless with regard to our most urgent problems? Are our best brains, our experts at the end of their rope?
Let us improve the lives of our citizens. Let production meet the needs of the people in their homes. This is possible. For that we only have to put at the disposal of Canadians the necessary purchasing power.
If society is able to provide the arms and the brains, it is the duty of governments to provide individuals with the purchasing power necessary to their development.
If, Mr. Speaker, interest rates on capital are too high, let us lower them. No one in this parliament has asked to lower the rates of interest which are too high, to bring to reason finance companies. There is no one either among the Liberals or among the Conservatives who would have the courage to ask that order be restored to the economic situation.
It is absurd that capital assets should always be more protected than human capital. Men are neglected but the golden calf -or is it made of silver or bronze-is always protected.
In 1964, Mr. Speaker, the total amount of taxes paid by the taxpayers exceeded what the citizens had spent for food, clothing and housing.
In 1964, each taxpayer paid about $800 out of his income solely for the federal government administration, that is almost 20 per cent of the average wage which is $4,200. It is a real shame. It is perfectly absurd. This, Mr. Speaker, is not the way to solve the problems of poverty amidst plenty.
On many occasions, I directed some questions to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) as well as to the government. I asked for an increase in family allowances, and the reply was that the government was considering the opportunity of increasing family allowances in order that they may be attuned to the tempo of the other sections of the national economy.
Do not forget that an eight-year old child, for instance, receives from our governments an allowance of $6 if he lives with his family, $65 in a foster home and up to $90 and $120 in orphanages and institutions. Such differences are recognized as normal and legitimate. These figures may be checked. They are a matter of public record. Why not
The Address-Mr. Latulippe increase family allowances to bring them in line with the rise in the cost of living?
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we wanted to bring family allowances in line with the cost of living, they would have to be at least $1 per day. The reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and of the Prime Minister is always about the same, vague and non-committal.
The government is always on the look-out for means to improve social security programs in Canada, and any decision in this respect will be announced in due course.
This is a word-for-word quotation from the debates of the House of Commons.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Since July 1944, that is since the enactment of the legislation, family allowances have remained at the same level, namely $6 and $8 per month, while in all other sectors of the economy, everything was multiplied by four, six, eight, ten and 11 as statistics show clearly. Why not the same escalation when human beings are concerned, especially when our children, the future citizens of Canada, are concerned?
In Canada, in 1964-65, there is no shortage of goods, housing, clothing, food or medical care. All that is plentiful. Manufacturers and businessmen want to sell, families have obvious needs. Nevertheless, the products are not sold according to the needs because of a lack of money in the family. The responsibility to remedy such a situation by restoring the proper balance of the economy rests with the government; that would give the consumers, our Canadian families, a purchasing power equal to the production yields.
What have you done, Grits or Tories, what solutions have you offered in these so-called 20 years of progress, so that the people could live according to the production capacity of the country, and not according to restrictions imposed by those who control money and credit? You have done nothing except increase our debt and consolidate the position of the financial dictatorship. During all that time, the only thing you did was to rob some to enable others to live or exist.
You have done nothing to make the material development work for Canadian individuals and families.
All that was done was to take note of the representations and suggestions of the people which means that nobody really deals with them, and for the people, the only alternative will be to live in patience or to die of despair.
April 8. 1965

The Address-Mr. Latulippe
It is easy to stifle the efforts of the awakeners of the masses. Mouldering in forced idleness and insecurity, are not those people ripe to accept anything?
You members of old-line parties you are responsible for the present chaos, you are responsible for the waste of the precious time we would have to find a solution to the defects of the economy. Certainly, it will be necessary some day to find a financial machine which will help Canadians, instead of punishing them, a machine which will make money to meet requirements, instead of merely creating debts; a machine which will increase purchasing power as the people increase production, instead of reducing this power through ever increasing taxes, without consideration for human beings.
Mr. Speaker, the right to life, the right to the means of living is a birthright, a right which implies the duty to respect the same right of others, by allowing them a reasonable standard of living, in a country where there is plenty of everything and where goods and skills are lost for lack of financial means. An addition to a family should not deprive the other members of the family or of the country of a decent livelihood.
Mr. Speaker, I ask this question. In order to benefit from the progress of science, to get three meals a day, is it necessary to be a dog? If not, let something be done.
Mr. Speaker, there is injustice in taxation; large institutions are favoured at the expense of private citizens. This is done to protect once more capital and especially interest.
In this way, companies and large institutions are afforded more opportunities to increase their dividends so that their shares may rise on the stock market. All that concerns only 10 per cent of the population; the mighty, the rich and the learned in Canada. All that gives nothing to the 80 per cent that forms the bulk of the people. Here we represent the people, we must see that they get justice, security and liberty.
Here are some very definite examples where the government grants great privileges to companies, while denying them to individuals.
First, the tax form for 1962 shows that companies pay only 21 per cent on their profits on the first $35,000 and only 50 per cent above $35,000 and there is no limitation, while individuals pay 50 per cent as soon as their taxable income has reached $25,000 and up to 80 per cent on larger sums.

Second, between 1954 and 1963, during a ten-year period of prosperity, the personal income tax went up by over $1,000 million whereas the corporation income tax remained at the same level, as can be seen on page 1041 of the French edition of The Canada Year Book, at approximately $116 million.
In the field of national economy, Mr. Speaker, before 1962, under various old age assistance programs, monthly payments of $20 or $25 to $40 were made to needy older citizens who presented an application and submitted to a means test.
In 1952, the government set up old age security, thus guaranteeing a pension of $40 a month to any person of 70 or over, without any means test.
That pension was raised to $46, on July 1, 1957, and to $55 on November 1 of the same year. On February 1, 1962, it was further increased to $65 a month and then again to $75 on October 1, 1963.
Consequently, old age security was raised in 1952, 1957, 1962 and 1963, five increases from 1952 to 1963.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Members' indemnities, including expense allowances, which were $4,000 in 1944, were raised to $18,000 in 1963. In fact, this indemnity which was $2,500 in 1906, $4,000 in 1920, $6,000 in 1945, $10,000 in 1954, is now $18,000.
On the other hand, family allowances, voted in 1944 and paid since July 1945, were $5, $6, $7 and $8 for children under 16. This was raised from $6 to $8 in 1957, before the surprise election called by the Right Hon. Leader of the present Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). This increase represented, on the average, one cent per day or 30 cents per month, for every child under 16. On the other hand, from 1944 to 1957, the price of milk went up five cents a quart.
Mr. Speaker, nothing was done on behalf of the families, on behalf of those who are the nation, the real nation, on behalf of the survival of Canadians, and toward the development of French Canadians. Nothing was done apart from levying new taxes, imposing new burdens and vexations. Those are the only achievements of our governments during 33 years of Liberal administration and during the rest of the time by the Conservative administration.
No one ever paid any attention to the people. However, many schemes were devised. Every possible formula and means
April 8, 1965

were found to wage war, to promote the expansion of high finance and the good of barons of finance. Measures were taken to favour only the powerful, to increase the rates of interest and to endorse loans for provinces, municipalities and school boards. We have come to the point where we are now endorsing for individuals. The only thing the federal government can do is to become an endorser and to adopt a patronizing attitude toward the large financial institutions, to the prejudice of the family.
After 33 years of Liberal administration, we are beginning to notice a feeling of unrest within society and to be aware of the need for reforms. But should those reforms be carried out by taking more money out of the pockets of the taxpayer, who has not enough already, how is this going to straighten out matters? The reforms proposed by this government will come to nothing.
The speech from the throne is vague and contains no concrete solution. The solutions that are being proposed and the reforms that are mentioned are general reforms. They are not likely to benefit the individual, the family; they do not tend to protect the family, in brief those who need to be protected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion proposed by the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and seconded by the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien). Both gentlemen discharged the traditional duties assigned to them with impressive eloquence. Reflecting upon the work and exhausting efforts of the past two sessions, the hon. Member for St. John's West chose this occasion to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). He said that the Prime Minister had shown a rare and perceptive talent for dealing with particular and urgent problems of this nation. Today, I add that the contents of the Speech from the Throne eloquently support that conclusion. The hon. Member for St. John's West went on to say that the Prime Minister was acutely aware of the situations in Canada and is magnificently equipped to deal with them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, events of the past few days have focused attention on the performance of Canada's Prime Minister. Canadians, and indeed people throughout the entire
The Address-Mr. Lloyd world, recently watched with great concern the escalation of the war in Viet Nam. All were grateful when Canada's Prime Minister, in a speech in Philadelphia, put forward constructive proposals that might remove another threat to world peace. Our thankfulness deepened yesterday when we learned that the President of the United States had shifted the emphasis of the United States from military to diplomatic measures in Southeast Asia. The Ottawa Citizen of April 8 reports the news in these words:
President Johnson has broken the impasse over Viet Nam with a declaration of willingness to hold "unconditional discussions" for a peaceful settlement.
He also proposed a vast Southeast Asian development scheme to which he said the U.S. would contribute one billion dollars as a starter.
The latter idea was phrased in almost the same terms used by Prime Minister Pearson last week.
It was a time of greatness, Mr. Speaker. Two men, President Johnson and Prime Minister Pearson, exhibited to the world that they possessed that quality when it was urgently needed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne contained many references to international matters; and the meaningfulness of this, as well as of the reality and the need to be involved in these affairs, was very well illustrated in the past few days. In addition, the Speech from the Throne deals with matters of development in Canada. We are concerned with the problems and factors of economic growth. There will be no easy answer to the challenge put to us by the Economic Council. Indeed, it would be absolutely foolish for us to expect that the solution we require to meet that challenge will be found simply and only in some tinkering with credit. It goes far beyond the question of credit.
Let us examine what the Economic Council has to say, and the effect that involvement in their proposals may have on urban regions of Canada and the rural areas of this country. Last December the Economic Council of Canada published its first annual review. The Council projected the expansion of the labour force and population growth through to 1970. By 1970 it is expected that over one million persons will be added to the labour force. The dominant factor, the report points out, is an increase in Canada's population of working age. Reflecting the high birth rate in the ten years following the war, the number of people in the 20 to 24 age group is expected to increase by 33 per cent from 1965

April 8. 1965
The Address-Mr. Lloyd to 1970. By the end of the decade, the increase will be 55 per cent. The average increase in the sixties of the 20 to 24 age group will be ten times that of the fifties.
The Council noted another significant element of change in the labour force. Ten years from now three out of ten married women are expected to be in the labour force, compared with only one out of ten in the fifties. The population of Canada last year crossed the 19 million mark. By 1970 we can reach 22 million, and the decade of the sixties will roughly see an increase of 22 per cent. The Economic Council continues to observe that with the massive inflow of young people, the rapid increase in the number of working wives, the labour force is expected to grow at a faster pace than the population. Speaking of the increase in labour force, allowance must be made for a reduction in the current rate of unemployment. The challenging conclusion by the Council is an additional 1.5 million jobs between 1963 and 1970.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
In the light of that realistic appraisal the justification for the much debated Canada Pension Plan became apparent. The funds it accumulates over the next ten to 15 years will be fully required to supplement the massive social capital needs of the Provinces and their municipalities in making their contribution to the essential growth of the economy. It is also clear that the portable benefits at age 65 of the Canada Pension Plan phased into maximum payments over the next ten years is a practical and timely measure. The same observation applies to the reduction of the retirement test of the Old Age Security benefit from age 70 to age 65 over the next five years. Competition for jobs in the next decade will make it increasingly difficult for our citizens of retirement age to obtain and hold remunerative employment. It should be noted that over 60 per cent of our labour force are not covered by private pension plans.
I was pleased to note that in the Speech from the Throne reference is made to the need for us to become involved in legislation which will bring about a consolidation of a number of assistance plans and bring about an improvement in the assistance provided under existing arrangements. The scheme is to be called the Canada Assistance Plan. There is no doubt in my mind that this is the next step to be taken. Those of us who were actively concerned with the Canada Pension Plan recognized that it needed to be done.

We thought that before increasing flat rate benefits we should take a first step with the Canada Pension Plan and then go on to a second stage, one to proceed concurrently with the pension plan itself.
Between 1963 and 1970 the pace of expansion will need to be substantially better than our longer run experience if we are to avoid severe social and economic problems and strains. What will be the impact of economic growth on our municipalities? The assumptions made by the Economic Council allow for a high and sustained rate of growth in investment in social capital. The Council recognized a high income society, demanded improved schools, hospitals, highways, streets, parks, cultural and recreational facilities. The report of the Council stated: "There is particular need to improve our cities for both economic and social reasons." The report continues:
This requires among other things rehabilitation of dilapidated residential areas or clearing of some of these areas for more efficient use for commercial and other purposes. There is the need for improved living conditions for families and individuals who are now relegated by economic circumstances and urban decay to substandard and blighted living conditions. To attempt to deal in a comprehensive manner with these needs will require the development of policies and programs directed towards the elimination of their underlying causes. Many problems exist in this field and available information about them is meagre. But we believe that it is essential to develop a much larger and more effective program than now exists for urban renewal and low rental housing.
As to this statement that available information is meagre, I have some reservations at this point about the extent of the Council's research work. Nevertheless, I will continue, my intention being to make some observations to show that the Economic Council might have gone further in its study of the problems of urban and rural municipalities and their relationship with the Provinces. It might have examined the situation in an effort to find out whether or not the provinces have plenty on their platter at home to deal with in the next decade without handing them long range plans having to do with constitutional amendments which will work well only when we work for common objectives regardless of what lawyers may write into those documents.
All of us have used expressions relating to automation and our rapidly changing technology. The latter phrase has become a cliche. But we all recognize what it means. We have observed the shift of population to the urban growth centres from the rural
April 8, 1965

areas. The urban population explosion is widened by the rapid growth of suburban districts, with their inevitable neighbourhood shopping centres.
It is in the urban areas that increasing numbers of employables seek jobs in the servicing sector of our economy, including recreation and the entertainment fields. It is in the metropolitan regions that we find extensive expansion of office buildings and high rise apartments. With the development of industrial parks to escape high central city taxes and land costs on the fringes of the expanded urban areas, workers find themselves no longer in suburbia. Many now leave their jobs to return to sleep and relax in the densely populated traffic-congested city.
In 1956 the City of Halifax decided to take full advantage of the provisions of the National Housing Act administered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We learned many lessons, experienced disappointments, and enjoyed some achievements. With C.M.H.C. paying half the cost of clearance we demolished several areas of badly blighted real estate. I could tell Hon. Members more about the details, but it suffices now to reach the point at which the bulldozer had completed its work on the first clearance area. The time had come to direct our attention to redevelopment. We soon learned that a comprehensive plan required a study of the economic base of the metropolitan region in which the city was located. We had to identify possible developments of highways and railroads to the region, and bridges to the city of Dartmouth on the eastern side of the harbour and across the North West Arm to county suburban districts. We recognized that, if we were to interest large private developers, economic data and other pertinent information about the city's services and regional developments were essential for that purpose.
We publicized invitations to developers to rebuild the site with broad terms of reference. We favoured leasing the site, because of apparent financial advantages to the city and to developers. To those who may become involved in this kind of thing I would suggest it might be wise to examine the value of a freehold type of lease, even though there may be advantages attached to leases of the more usual kind. We received one proposal from a British consortium of professional planners. They proposed high density development of
The Address-Mr. Lloyd a mixture of tall tower apartment buildings, shopping, banking and office buildings. We decided to negotiate an agreement with our only customer. The proposals were redesigned and scaled down to correspond with both good planning and conservation of economic feasibility.
We discovered a number of things. We found that the cleared site was too isolated from the central business district, requiring the developer to acquire and clear blighted commercial districts to appropriately link the new developments with existing and well developed sectors of the central city region. After many, many months of detailed construction planning for the site, and negotiating of legal agreements with developers, they found they could not complete, to the city's satisfaction, the necessary evidence of financial capability to complete their $30 million undertaking.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Now they must make a fresh start. In the meantime, Webb and Knapp built a $9 million shopping centre in the west end of the City, with Eaton's abandoning their downtown store to become the key tenant. Simpson's across the road, rehabilitated their buildings to meet the competition. Across the harbour in Dartmouth, an industrial complex development stimulated with financial assistance from Provincial Crown Corporations, Industrial Estates Ltd., and low municipal taxes. Dartmouth has been compelled in turn to undertake development land use planning to ensure orderly expansion and redevelopment within its boundaries.
Stimulated by the flow of information on the factors or urban growth and the economic prospects of the region, local realtors and others acquired and cleared sites for high rise apartments and office buildings. The pressure for high density development to offset high cost of land acquisition and local taxes produced many conflicts between the City's planning staff and the private developers. Despite these difficulties much better redevelopment of the city has been accomplished. We are pleased to observe that last year the Federal Government amended its legislation on urban renewal. C.M.H.C. is authorized to extend its participation in clearance cost of blighted commercial districts. That Federal corporation will share the cost of providing sewers, streets, etc. to the cleared redevelopment site, thus relieving the developer from that burden of investment.

speechtext:
I hope he will take the advice, too; and I am sure he will. These economic advisers had this to say:
Mobility is necessary. There is no escape from that conclusion. But, if the policy of regional development succeeds, it should be possible to reduce the net outflow of population from the area as a whole. It is necessary to distinguish at this point-
April 8, 1965

I am sure some hon. Members would agree with this:
-between the Maritimes and Newfoundland. No doubt it is true that when a family has decided to leave the island, it is just as likely to move to Central Canada as to the Maritimes. Newfoundland must, therefore, rely upon the attractiveness of her own centre, or centres, of growth. But it seems true to say that people will move around within each province more readily than they would move to Central Canada.
Some of us in the Atlantic Provinces, of course, can fully understand why:
This is one reason why the development of provincial centres of growth should be a means of tapping resources of manpower that would otherwise remain idle or would continue to work in occupations where productivity was low. Quite a lot of this labour may, indeed, be within commuting distance of such appropriate centres as Halifax or Saint John.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I hope that when we reach that stage in our legislative process we will be considering amendments to the legislation we now have with respect to areas of slow growth; that we will keep in mind the lessons which have been learned by the municipalities; and that we will keep in mind what I have said this evening about the explosion in population, if you like, in the urban areas. We must be ready to provide jobs for the 1,500,000 people which the Economic Council says will be added to our labour force in the next five or six years.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Provinces as well as the municipalities have a job to do in this field. The Federal Government can help them with resources and with technical skill and advice; but the initiative must lie with the municipalities in this field and with a fully co-operating and understanding Provincial Government.
I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, and I can add only one further thought, which is this. Economic land use planning is just as essential in our rural areas of Canada, and this is a matter which should receive concurrent consideration by the Provincial Government. You cannot hope to have intelligent development and redevelopment planning in the urban areas of Canada without in turn examining what will be happening in the hinterland of these great areas of urban growth. So I welcome the obvious interest of the Canadian Government in the field of improvement in areas of slow growth and in the rural regions of Canada, as expressed through the ARDA program. But I must conclude with this observation, that it might be wise for all of us to remember
The Address-Mr. Rynard and to be somewhat humbled by this very complex business of economics. A great deal has been written on the subject, and there has been a great deal of advice from a number of people holding a wide variety of views. It seems to me that together we need to work and learn more if together we hope to progress in a better manner than has been the case in the past.

We have listened to a very informative and interesting speech on the problems of urban development and renewal, and while he had some very enlightening opinions respecting many of the problems which would be raised, it did seem to me that he had left out the central problem, which is raising the funds required. I was wondering whether he had any ideas about the changes which could be brought about to provide for this.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, remembering my closing observations about being humbled by the intricacies and complexities of economics, I am sure the Hon. Member who asked me the question on the matter of funding will appreciate my reply, which is this: We have given consideration to the matter of funding. One source of social capital for the kind of things about which I have been talking will be the funds raised by the Canada Pension Plan. There are others who advocate different viewpoints-that there should be a different use of Canada's credit facilities and expansion of its monetary supply.
