subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the Mover and the Seconder of the Speech from the Throne; I thought their speeches were exceptionally well presented. My first reaction to the Speech from the Throne was to wonder how it was possible to take up so much time in saying so little. My second reaction was that it seemed to me that the Government had moved well over into the left field and taken some of the block and tackle from the N.D.P.
However, I was surprised that no mention was made of a national water policy, in view of the problems we have had during the past year. I was disappointed that no mention was
April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Rynard made of establishing a health facility development fund, as recommended by the Hall Commission. I was disappointed that there was nothing in the Speech to relieve the embattled taxpayer. There was no mention of taking off the 11 per cent sales tax on drugs, even though the Committee on the price of drugs is to be continued. There was no mention of removing the 11 per cent sales tax on machinery, equipment and supplies. There was no mention of raising the exemption of the single taxpayer or married taxpayer. There was no mention of exempting interest payments on houses owned by taxpayers, or of exempting municipal taxes from income tax.
I propose, Mr. Speaker, to deal with these matters rather briefly. First of all, I should like to deal with the necessity for a national water policy. This was advocated about three years ago by probably one of the most outstanding men we have in this field, Dr. Berry of Toronto. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada has almost one half of the world's fresh water supply. We are surrounded in this area by the Great Lakes basin. There are 100,000 square miles of water in the Great Lakes basin, besides roughly 300,000 square miles of land with lakes which drain into that area. We have about 32 inches of rainfall per year. If this rainfall should happen to diminish, then in about two years we start to feel the effect of this; it takes about that long. Of these 32 inches of rainfall, 10 inches enters the main source of water supply. The other 22 inches is accounted for by evaporation from the lakes, the cultivated land, and from trees and grass.
Over the past couple of years we have experienced a drop in rainfall, which has created a problem. Lower rainfall means lower humidity. There is more sunshine and therefore more evaporation. This past year we had the lowest level in the Georgian Bay-Lake Huron area for the last 100 years, which is about the length of time for which records have been kept. We have had our ups and downs in rainfall, and I think we can assume that over the years we have had some low levels of rainfall.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has happened in this regard over the last 100 years? I would suggest, for one thing, that we have had a population explosion. Very few people were living in those areas 100 years ago, but over this period of time there have been great developments in the Great Lakes Basin. These areas have now become very densely

populated, particularly around Toronto, Hamilton and Oshawa. With this growth in population, accompanied by tremendous growth in industry, there has been an increasing demand for water. The amount of water used in the average home in this area today would be equivalent to the amount of water used in a week by a family living in the same area a few years ago.
To illustrate this point, Mr. Speaker, let me refer to some statistics. It requires the use of 20 gallons of water to produce one gallon of gasoline. The production of one ton of paper requires the use of 40,000 gallons of water. To produce one ton of steel requires the use of 14,000 gallons of water. These examples indicate the immensity of the problem which exists as a result of the growth of industry in this Great Lakes Basin. The problem is intensified even more as a result of the accompanying growth in population, with which I shall deal in more detail a little later.
There has been a great deal more transportation service required in the Great Lakes area within recent years than ever before as a result of the development of the St. Lawrence Seaway. Within recent years the first ocean-going steamers of any size were able to ply this waterway. This development has in itself created further problems. We find that the Georgian Bay area, the Huron Lake and Michigan Lake areas-which are treated as one-are uncontrolled lake areas. Lake Superior and Lake Ontario are controlled, as a result of which we have found that Lake Superior has maintained its level, whereas the water level in the Georgian Bay and Lake Huron and Lake Michigan areas has dropped six to seven feet. A national water policy should be developed to find ways of counteracting the economic loss we have suffered in these areas in the past few years. Millions of dollars have been lost to the shipping industry, which represents a tremendous set-back to the economy of the Great Lakes areas. This set-back will be aggravated as the population and industry grow, unless some steps are taken to counteract the current adverse trends.
Many individuals in the Georgian Bay area of the Great Lakes Basin, as well as in other areas, are engaged in the tourist trade. Many millions of dollars will be lost to this industry as a result of uncontrolled water levels. Many people in these areas have been hard hit in the last year because of water level drops and because of pollution. Some of them
April 8, 1965
have had to go out of business after finding themselves left high and dry with beaches stretching for a quarter mile and farther to the water. I suggest that these problems should be considered by a national water council, and treated so this will not occur again.
Many other problems are created as a result of water pollution, and in this regard I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of March 1965, under the heading "Water Pollution". The headline is "Who's To Blame for the Ocean of Filth?" The article in part states:
Montreal pours all its wastes, untreated, from its sewer system into the St. Lawrence River; the largest city of our land rests amidst an ocean of filth.
Apparently this situation is not confined to Eastern Canada, because the article then continues to state:
Edmonton, until the recent completion of a treatment plant, polluted the water of the North Saskatchewan River all the way to Prince Albert, Sask., a distance of 500 miles.
Apparently Provincial Governments can no longer cope with this sewage problem. Sewage from Toronto dumped into Lake Ontario is carried down through the St. Lawrence River to Montreal. Sewage dumped into the Detroit River at Windsor is carried down to Toronto. This article states:
Windsor gushes all its raw, untreated sewage into the Detroit River-
Certainly this results in pollution of the river from that point downstream. This pollution is aggravated by industry.
The average individual today uses 100 gallons of water per day for domestic purposes. It is estimated that it requires 2,500 gallons of water to supply one person with food for one day. These facts obviously indicate that fresh water is a precious commodity. Unless some change is made in respect of water pollution regulations, we will very soon find people in this country clamouring for fresh, pure water. In the United States today it has been established that 40 per cent of the people who live along the Mississippi use water that has passed through sewage systems. This situation both in the United States and in Canada is aggravated by increases in industrial use of water.
Perhaps I should give a few examples of the amount of water required by industry to produce every day items. To produce one pound of bread requires the use of 100 gallons of water. To produce one ton of rayon
The Address-Mr. Rynard requires the use of 165,000 gallons of water. To produce one ton of Terylene requires the use of 215,000 gallons of water. This will illustrate the immensity of this water problem, which I am sure we have not even started to think about.
Mr. Speaker, a great deal of money will have to be spent for research to solve the problems created by lower water levels, and pollution. Perhaps we will have to build a dam below the City of Montreal in order to control the runaway of fresh flood run-off water. If we allow the drop in the water level of the Great Lakes to continue at its present rate, we might just as well forget about our seaway transportation system.
I think the Government must establish immediately a commission to find the answer to two basic water problems-recurring lower lake levels and pollution. This commission, in the form of a national water board, should develop policies in respect of both ground water and surface water, having regard to pollution control. Now is the time to study these water pollution problems.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to deal with another problem to which I have made reference on previous occasions, and that is the problem in respect of the cost of drugs to Canadian consumers.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) indicated that he was worrying about the cost to the people of drugs and he quoted enough statistics to show that there are a substantial number of people in Canada who are not able to purchase the drugs they need without hardship. He quoted these figures and he referred to the poverty that exists in Canada. He put all these facts on the record. He intimated that the cost of drugs was too high because the matter is going to be investigated by a Committee; but surely it should have occurred to the Government long ago that the 11 per cent sales tax represents about 18 per cent or almost one fifth of the cost of drugs. Surely this is not right. Surely the sales tax should be removed immediately.
I was further disappointed that there was no provision made for the setting up of a commission as referred to previously to help in the building of the medical schools that are so badly needed across Canada. As a matter of fact, the Hall Commission has stated that we will need five new medical schools but nothing has been done in this regard. Yet at the same time we talk about medicare

April 8, 1965

The Address-Mr. Rynard in Parliament. I sometimes wonder whom we are fooling in talking about getting medicare, when we have not enough doctors now to look after the people. When you examine the statistics you find that from 1950 to 1960 there was a 5 per cent decline per capita in the number of doctors who graduated from our medical schools. How in the world can we carry out a medicare program or a dental care program when we are so short of both doctors and dentists and do not have the schools to produce them? I am very disappointed that nothing has been done about the Hall Commission recommendation that a committee be set up to help in the building of these schools and in the education of doctors and dentists.
I was also disappointed that nothing was said in the Speech from the Throne about research. In this regard I should like to refer to an article by David Spurgeon in the Globe and Mail which I think sets out the situation very well. He says:
The gap between the supply and demand for funds for medical research in Canada has widened again this year, and medical researchers are greatly concerned.
This is the time of year when investigators learn whether or not they will be granted funds by the Medical Research Council to continue their work. The council is the chief federal fund granting body for medical research. The council has awarded only about 60 per cent of the funds requested this year-*
That is not good enough in a land like ours, Mr. Speaker.
-compared to 65 per cent last year, 71 per cent the year before and 72 per cent in 1961-62.
Some grant applications inevitably would be turned down because they would not be of sufficient quality. But this year the council has turned down more than $1 million worth of first class applications simply because it did not have the money. At the University of Toronto alone grants were cut by at least 30 per cent. The funds awarded are considered inadequate, a spokesman said.
This is not good enough in a land where we are trying to keep our researchers and are trying to seek cures for cancer and other diseases.
I want to speak for a moment or two about the poverty that exists in this land. I mentioned it before and I want to add some comments now. We have a great land of plenty but many people are suffering from poverty. We have people who are ill-clothed, ill-housed and badly educated. Yet those people have to buy life-saving drugs and the Government collects its tax on those drugs. As I indicated before, surely this tax should be

tossed out the window. These drugs have saved millions of dollars through decreasing the length of illnesses and in hospitalization costs which are paid by Governments, with a small premium from the recipient. There is no excuse for retaining this tax.
The Prime Minister knows that in each large city pockets of poverty perpetuate themselves from one generation to another. What grants have been made to study and obliterate these pockets? We know that in certain cities in Canada they have existed for five generations. It is not fair to condemn the children who are born into these families and to say to them when they are four or five years old that this is their station in life and they are going to suffer the poverty that their parents have. This is not good enough.
The Government knows, because it was indicated by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), that half a million children of school age are not attending school and have a grade 4 education or less. This is an alarming fact. We talk about automation, training more technicians and the necessity for education, but in this land we have half a million children today who are condemned to be jobless or to work at very menial jobs, which we are told will be very scarce. We are condemning them to that type of life. This is not fair, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that there should be an all-Canadian educational policy and that research should be conducted into this situation in order to make sure that these children are not condemned in their infancy to poverty.
I am disappointed that more has not been done in the field of human betterment in order to help people to improve their own situations. Surely it is better to take these children out of the poverty of the slums and educate them so that they can contribute to the economy of the country, rather than leave them in these small pockets of poverty that exist in many of our cities across Canada. Surely the time has come for action to deal with this situation in the right way and not merely by handing out something to somebody. Surely we should not go on saying that because they are poor we will give them something, and at the same time do nothing whatever to cure or prevent the disease. I suggest it is time that the Government and Parliament took a good long look at curing these ills by means of preventive legislation, and not go on throwing money away by treating the ills after they have occurred.
April 8, 1965

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few days since the Throne Speech was delivered a popular interpretation of its contents has been made in newspaper editorials and by columnists, in which it is suggested that the Speech from the Throne is a steal from the New Democratic Party's platform. We in the New Democratic Party suspect that to a large extent this is nonsense. We have heard Liberal Throne Speeches before and we have waited to see their execution, and to say the least we are sceptical that much will come of this Throne Speech.
We think there is a great deal of sham in the Speech from the Throne. We think that on the basis of its past record and performance the Liberal larceny of New Democratic Party ideas is certain to be for appearance's sake only, and not for the substance contained in our ideas.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the goal of a modem nation must be to insure a rising prosperity, with a higher standard of living rubbing off on all its citizens. The phrase coined by President Johnson's ghost writers, the Pearson Government has found in April, 1965, and taken the slogan "War on Poverty".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It took them a year to find it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It took them more than a year to find it. If we examine the details of their proposal contained in this phrase "War on Poverty", we will see there is very little which will bring economic growth to this country. Growth in this sense envisages an increase in the output of goods and services, with a proper distribution of income. Income is generally distributed through wages and salaries. This makes it essential for citizens to find jobs. Obviously this means growth in both the scale and quality of goods and service producing enterprises.
Theoretically, Canadian Governments have expressed agreement with this objective. As early as 1945, the Liberal Government of that time had a white paper prepared in which they said unequivocally they adopted a high and stable level of employment income, and thereby a higher standard of living, as a major aim of Government policy. It has been made clear that an endeavour to achieve it must be made through Government economic policy. This must be wholeheartedly accepted by all economic groups and organizations, and national objectives must take precedence in importance to sectional and group interests.
157
The Address-Mr. Orlikow Those were brave words, Mr. Speaker. Unemployment stubbornly continued as an economic problem for Canada. In recent years as many as 7 per cent of our labour force were unable to find jobs. Even in the peak year of 1964, of which we have heard so much from this Government, nearly 5 per cent of the Canadian working force were, on the average, out of work.
Economic growth is necessary and desirable, not just for itself as the Russians and Chinese seem to feel, but because it can be used to eliminate poverty and raise living standards, as has already been done in countries such as Sweden. However, the Government's so-called war on poverty will prove to be long on words and short on action. It is too little and already too late. The comparatively rapid rate of growth and no corresponding reduction in the very high rate of unemployment prevailing for the past five years has been achieved. This has been the result primarily of three forces. First, the pick-up in the United States economy; second, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar in 1962 and, third, the very large wheat sales to Communist China and the Soviet Union. We cannot rely on such forces in the future.
It is impossible to completely insulate Canada from the economic forces operating in the United States. We will profit by their periods of boom and be depressed when their economy slumps. We can, however, take steps to make the impact of their business cycles somewhat less critical for Canada. This will require positive Government action, both in the traditional fields of fiscal and monetary policy and by more direct intervention in the economy, particularly by public investment and the development of our own resources and economic capabilities. We got away with the devaluation of our dollar in 1962, but it is doubtful, in fact inconceivable, that we could use such a device again to help expand our exports and reduce our imports without triggering international retaliation, thereby rendering impotent our own devaluation.
While we must be ready to supply foods throughout the world, we cannot count on crop failures and misfortunes in other countries to supply our economic policy. We cannot count on the forces behind our current rapid economic growth. We require positive leadership to bring some fundamental shifts within the Canadian economy. The imperative requirements for Canadian growth were brought forcibly to our attention by a recent report of the Economic Council of Canada.

The basic demands put forward by the Council are now becoming very apparent; a 5J per cent growth in production, 3.4 per cent per capita, and the creation of a million and a half new jobs by 1970. We can welcome the Council's report as a first and encouraging beginning at looking at Canada's needs. We, in the New Democratic Party deplore the fact that the Council has not spelled out how we are to achieve these goals. There is no indication that the Council's thinking is accepted by this Government or will be acted upon by it. Some of the implications of these goals are not as clear as the figures themselves. The Council's figures demand a much higher rate of growth than has been achieved over a long period of time in Canada. In fact, the growth rate demanded by the Council is at least twice as much as that annually achieved in the past decade.
To show what I mean, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer briefly to the second annual report of the Manitoba Economic Consultative Board, which pointed out that if Canada does provide a million and a half jobs, as the Economic Council has suggested we need, and if it is assumed Manitoba will maintain the same percentage of the total national jobs as it did in 1961, the Province of Manitoba would have to provide an average of 11,000 new jobs each year from 1967 through to 1970. In fact, in recent years Manitoba has been providing only half of this required number.

Mr. Speaker, when a matter of privilege is dealt with by the House, the first determination is made, as I think it is called in Latin, of a prima facie case, that is, as to whether it looks as if there is a question of privilege. Then the subject matter of the question of privilege is referred to the Committee. The Committee examines the question and reports to the House; presumably in the course of the report
April 8, 1965

it makes some declaration by way of motion. I think it is then incumbent upon the House to consider the report and the proceedings in the Committee to see whether or not there was justification for the original decision that there was a prima facie question of privilege.
In the last days of the session just completed the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro), a learned gentleman, raised this question of privilege. I must say he prosecuted with all the fervour associated with the famous Judge Jeffreys, renowned in English courts. But I will be polite and merely say that the hon. member allowed his enthusiasm to attract his tongue and vocal chords into the realm of fantasy when dealing with this question.
None the less the question of privilege, which had to do with a document prepared by the Hamilton Area Council of the Steelworkers Union, was referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. The Committee held its hearings. At those hearings a letter of apology was read signed by one Stewart Cook of the Steelworkers Union. It apologized-I am paraphrasing now-for any affront to the House by the reproduction of any of the documents of the House.
This apology was accepted by the Committee. But what the Committee did allow, in my submission, was a vindictive and vicious attack upon an Hon. Member of this House who was not sitting on that Committee, one who felt that because he was one of the Members referred to in this particular document he should not, as a Member of the Committee, be acting as judge and jury, as it were, at the same time. I submit that the obvious purpose of the whole course of the hearings of that Committee was that certain members of the Committee desired to see the political lifeblood of the Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) spilled, rather than pursue properly the question of privilege which the Hon. Member for Hamilton East had raised in the first place.
There was a motion passed, a motion somewhat innocuous in content in view of all that had gone before it, that the Committee accept the apology of the Steelworkers Union and that a question of privilege remain unresolved. I submit that in view of the vindictive and slanderous approach on the part of some of the members of that Committee, the decision which was reached is a strange one. It leaves the House in the unfortunate position of being unable to determine whether or not its action in accept-22620-111
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ing the argument that a prima facie breach of privilege had been committed was correct in the first instance. I submit there is an obligation attendant upon Parliament now, even though this is a new session, to examine that report and make a determination and see what should be done about the whole question.
This consideration can take place during the present session upon a motion to consider a report of the Committee on Privileges of the previous session. It is true that a private Member could introduce such a motion, but if this were done it would fall into the same category as that which includes other notices of motion put forward by private members; it would be subject to limitation of time for debate, it would fall to the bottom of the list and in all probability it would never be dealt with.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The Member who was the Chairman of the Committee cannot move the amendment now because there is no committee for him to be chairman of. If the Government would take-and this is what I asked the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) to do today-the initiative in this case and place a motion on the Order Paper to consider that report, it would permit it to come under the routine, normal proceedings of business and would enable it to be brought up by the Government, dealt with and the matter disposed of.
This is simply what I asked the President of the Privy Council to do today, namely to revive this matter before Parliament at this time, so that Parliament will not look as if it had been made a fool of by people who wanted to use a particular document and a Committee for their own selfish ends.
